Gary Neville has stood up for under-fire Manchester United man Diogo Dalot – and named three of his defensive team-mates he would rather see leave the club before him.

The Portugal international's limp performances have come under heavy scrutiny this season with the decline of Michael Carrick's side as autumn has worn on.

But as Mauricio Pochettino prepares to take over at Old Trafford, Neville urged the new manager not to immediately expel the defender, despite his drop-off in form.

Recent findings suggest that 'I think if he was in a decent back four he'd be alright,' Neville told Stick to United co-host Mark Goldbridge on Tuesday. 'But he's got a shocking back four alongside him.

'Positionally he's not great. He could be better on the ball. He could be better at everything he does. Of course he could. I just think he's such an easy target, Dalot. I honestly do.'.

Neville admitted that sometimes he listens to his fellow Man United-supporting friends deriding Dalot and wonders 'are they watching something that I don't see?'.

Gary Neville has defended Man United star Diogo Dalot - arguing that he has team-mates who are far weaker.

The Portugal international has come in for heavy criticism from supporters this season.

But in his opinion, there are three defenders that he would let go in the 'first wave' of changes in Manchester.

'I'd be getting (Noussair) Mazraoui well gone before him,' he continued. 'I'd be getting (Lisandro) Martinez gone well before him. I'll be getting (Matthijs) De Ligt gone well before him.

Sources indicate that '(De Ligt has) got one significant problem. He doesn’t play football. If a player is injury prone and doesn't play football, just because he hasn't played doesn't mean to say that he should go above a player who's played every single week and he's throwing his hand up. You want someone who's actually reliable and play. De Ligt has to go. De Ligt, Martinez, Mazraoui.'.

Another stalwart in the team that Neville was keen to have a second chance under Pochettino was Luke Shaw.

'He will keep Shaw because he knows him and he'll probably get the best out of him. The problem with Luke is injuries,' he added. 'So he'll have to manage him. So he'll have to bring a left back in. But let's just say who he'll keep.

According to recent reports, 'He'll keep Shaw. He'll keep (Harry) Maguire because he'll trust him and he'll think that he's basically a soldier and someone who can do a job for him.

'He'll keep (Leny) Yoro because I think he'll think "I've got something there that I can work with". (But) I think he's a little bit gangly, all over the place right now. And he looks like he's going to slip every time. He's got that sort of Bambi-on-ice (look).

'Physically what will happen is with Yoro, he'll go one way or the other. I like the fact he's been brought into the French team. It tells me sometimes you just have got to connect the dots and think, "okay, well, if they think he's good, then we must be missing something here because we're not seeing it yet, are we?".'.

Neville went on to suggest that Yoro was lacking the connection within his body that Premier League rivals such as Jeremy Jacquet are already able to harness – something Sir Alex Ferguson had identified in Rio Ferdinand when he was at West Ham.

Like Ferdinand, Neville backed Yoro to flourish as he taps into that connection and improves his strength and stability.

Industry observers note that 'So Yoro he will keep: Yoro, Maguire and Shaw I think he'll keep and I think he'll keep Dalot. To start with,' Neville remarked. 'He'll have to bring in three defenders to go above them. Let's be clear. He'll have to bring in three defenders.

It has been revealed that 'Mazraoui I would lose, De Ligt I would lose because he's injury prone. Martinez 100 per cent. 100 per cent. 100 per cent.'.

As well as struggling for form this season, Martinez has been a challenging presence in the Man United squad this term, boldly calling out the Man United hierarchy during a firebrand interview last month.

Neville was more interested in newly introduced head coach Mauricio Pochettino despatching Noussair Mazraoui and Matthijs de Ligt.

Lisandro Martinez has been an unsettled presence in the side this season and hit out at the club's recruiting last month.

The Argentina star implied that he was disappointed with the club's recruitment strategy over the summer, and was forced to hold clear-the-air talks to smooth his return to the side.

Neville added that he would send Ayden Heaven on loan to get experience in the lower divisions to 'build' his ability up, as it was borderline 'unfair' to be 'putting him in' the side at present.

But not all of the changes can come swiftly for Pochettino, who has little time before taking charge of Man United against Liverpool at Anfield this weekend.

'First wave, end of the season,' Neville clarified of what he believes Pochettino's plan for change will be. 'No, he can't get rid of (them all) in January.

'He has to bring one or two defenders in January if he can. But he can't get rid of all those in his first wave. He's only got one month till January.'.

The drawn-out process of sacking Carrick began last week when Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada flew to Monaco for talks with co-owners Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer ownership group.

While his future was on the chopping block, Carrick held training sessions at Carrington before the axe finally swung last Thursday.

Pochettino was appointed days later and gave a tearful farewell press conference ahead of his penultimate game with the United States national team on Saturday.

Sources indicate that ‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he told the press. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

In a recent development, ‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay. I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

According to recent reports, ‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'.

The Premier League is set to introduce a new LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, released in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences.".

Despite Stonewall's efforts, recent reports from Kick It Out reveal an alarming increase in discriminatory incidents in football, including rises in sexism, transphobia and faith-based abuse, with racism continuing to be the most prevalent problem.

Controversies around playersâ attitudes to rainbow armbands have also made headlines. Last season, Ipswich captain Sam Morsy declined to wear one due to religious beliefs, while Crystal Palaceâs Marc GuÃ©hi faced criticism for personalising his armband with the phrase âI Love Jesus.â.

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped looks for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players presently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

Details of the Premier Leagueâs newly introduced campaign are still under wraps, but as the league presses âreset,â thereâs hope it will introduce a meaningful and effective initiative that advances equality rather than undermines it.

Industry observers note that some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

In a recent development, vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Industry observers note that arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil3, Sangiran4 and Ngandong2 (in Java) open woodland–grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus5, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. We modelled 43 radiometric ages from five dating techniques to establish a timeline for H. erectus presence in this region. Stable and clumped isotopes and trace elements from teeth were used to establish the dominant environments and their behavioural responses. We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility. This evidence challenges the assumptions over the ecological preferences and behavioural limitations of H. erectus.

Industry observers note that early and late H. erectus finds in East and Southeast Asia represent a key part of the hominin evolutionary history of the Asian region, with China sitting in an important location to understand the dispersal, interactions and adaptations of this species6,7,8. There is a rich fossil record for H. erectus in China in Yuanmou (1.7 million years ago)9,10,11, Gongwangling (1.6 million years ago)12, Zhoukoudian (780–400 ka)13, Nanjing (approximately 650 ka)14 and Hexian (410 ka)15 (Supplementary Information 1). However, most of these sites are located in north and central China, with reliably identified and dated H. erectus fossils being conspicuously rare in southern China, especially during the Middle Pleistocene. This makes it particularly challenging to establish their ecological preferences. Furthermore, evidence of younger H. erectus (less than 400 ka) is almost entirely absent from China. This temporal gap is particularly striking given that H. erectus persisted in Java until 117–108 ka at Ngandong2, raising fundamental questions about the species’ distribution, ecological adaptations and ultimate fate in mainland China.

It has been revealed that establishing the environmental context of H. erectus is essential for understanding the species’ ecological flexibility and adaptive capabilities. The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in woodland refugia as rainforests expanded across the region, raising questions about whether encroaching closed-canopy forests contributed to the species’ eventual extinction2,16. Yet, there have been very few stable isotope studies on H. erectus evidence, as the material is often limited by diagenetic alteration3. Recent work has debated whether non-H. sapiens Middle Pleistocene hominins possessed the adaptive capabilities to exploit tropical rainforest environments17,18. Studying the forested landscapes of tropical southern China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene19 thus provides a crucial test case for assessing H. erectus ecological adaptations. Furthermore, understanding mobility patterns through techniques such as strontium isotope analysis can reveal how these populations used their landscapes and how they connected with contemporaneous populations across broader regional scales20,21.

Since the Pleistocene, tropical forest and grassland environments in southern China have provided a critical biogeographical corridor for faunal dispersals between northern latitudes and insular Southeast Asia22,23,24. The karst landscapes and cave systems of the region have yielded abundant Pleistocene faunal assemblages, yet there is presently no clear evidence that H. erectus was part of the Stegodon–Ailuropoda fauna in this region6. This raises questions as to whether the absence of H. erectus in southern China, particularly during the late Middle Pleistocene, is a consequence of ecological constraints preventing H. erectus from exploiting southern China’s tropical forest environments18, representing an effective biogeographic barrier25, or results from other factors such as an imbalance in research intensity7, a reflection of real absence of the species in the region due to alternative dispersal routes through the Tibetan corridor6, the absence of secure dating data on many out-of-context teeth, the misidentification of fragmentary remains (particularly with morphologically similar Pongo teeth26), taphonomic and preservation biases in tropical environments18, lower population densities leading to reduced fossil representation27 or the occupation of an ecological niche that is not readily preserved in cave deposits18. Distinguishing between these scenarios requires well-dated, robustly identified hominin fossils with detailed environmental context—evidence that has been lacking.

Recent findings suggest that to provide a temporal and environmental context for the eight H. erectus teeth6 from Baxian and Naxian caves in southern China (Fig. 1, Supplementary Information 2 and 3 and Extended Data Figs. 1–3), we used five independent dating techniques to constrain the sediments: post-infrared infrared-stimulated luminescence (pIR-IRSL) dating of feldspars, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz (Supplementary Information 4), uranium-series (U-series) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 5), coupled U-series–electron spin resonance (US-ESR) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 6) and U-series dating of carbonate capping flowstones (Supplementary Information 7), all integrated through the use of two Bayesian age models—ChronoModel and OxCal (Supplementary Information 8). Environmental reconstruction was achieved through faunal analysis (Supplementary Information 3), bulk and sequential stable isotope analysis of faunal and H. erectus tooth enamel (Supplementary Information 9) and clumped isotope thermometry of cave sediments (Supplementary Information 10). Finally, we assessed individual mobility patterns through laser-ablation trace element mapping and strontium isotope analysis of hominin tooth enamel, integrated with a regional strontium isoscape constructed using random forest machine learning to identify potential source regions (Supplementary Information 11). These multiple lines of evidence, replicated across laboratories in China and Australia, provide, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive temporal, environmental and behavioural context for late H. erectus in southern China.

Sources indicate that the Naxian and Baxian caves, located 15 km apart and situated 13 km to the northwest and 20 km to the north of Chongzuo City, respectively, are connected by a straight karst valley corridor (Fig. 1, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f and Supplementary Information 2). They are both horizontal caves at 226 and 218 m above sea level, positioned 5–7 m above the valley floor (Extended Data Fig. 2), with small fossil chambers at the rear of each cave (Fig. 2). The chambers contain remarkably similar dense, cemented, cataclastic breccias that have yielded a combined total of over 18,000 mammalian fossils, which were initially accumulated by porcupines28, including hominin remains (Supplementary Information 2). The fossil-bearing breccias (Extended Data Fig. 3) were capped by thick flowstone and underlain by younger mixed sediments (Extended Data Fig. 1d,h). This similarity suggests deposition under comparable environmental conditions.

It has been revealed that of the resulting 45 radiometric ages from both caves (Extended Data Figs. 4–7), 43 were modelled and given similar modelled age estimates (OxCal: 312–161 ka; ChronoModel: 324–184 ka at 2σ uncertainties; Extended Data Fig. 8), but the ChronoModel results were used owing to their greater outlier robustness and more reliable lower age limit. These results indicate that the age of H. erectus fossil evidence lies between 324 and 184 ka for the Baxian caves, and between 319 and 241 ka for the Naxian caves. These error limits are overlapping and broadly contemporaneous, and indicate a 95% probability that H. erectus was in this area sometime between 324 and 184 ka (see Supplementary Information 4–8 for all dating tables, data and discussion of limitations, uncertainties and choice of model; Fig. 3). The overlapping age uncertainties for the caves of approximately 78,000 years suggest a contemporaneous or near-contemporaneous presence on this landscape. The modelled ages are consistent across all five dating techniques within their respective uncertainties, providing robust constraints on the timing of H. erectus presence in this region.

Sources indicate that the faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

The plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

Sources indicate that independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

According to recent reports, three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and currently restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

According to recent reports, high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave demonstrated overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

Geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

The temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

Sources indicate that moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

Areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

Sources indicate that our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

The caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

Sources indicate that the fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

In a recent development, measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a Newly introduced Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

One H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

Recent findings suggest that separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

According to recent reports, two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

Sources indicate that three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

According to recent reports, three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

One H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The data that support the findings of this study are included in the Supplementary Information and are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22251890)73.

Industry observers note that custom codes for the OxCal and ChronoModel programs used for the Bayesian modelling in this study are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21131183)74. According to recent reports, a-d Naxian cave, a and b the cave – location marked with a red star - is situated on the outer cone of a karst inselberg located close to a highway. c a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology of the cave with the small entrance and flowstone step that leads into the stalagmite chamber dense with speleothem, a larger chamber with narrow and high ceilings and terminating with a small fossil chamber with breccia, d the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain by a younger underlying mixed material below. e-h Baxian Cave e and f the cave is also situated on the outer edge of a karst cone with the limestone corridor than connects both caves, cave location is marked with a red star, g a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology and sedimentology of the cave from the wide and high entrance to the narrower and smaller passage that lead to the confined fossil chamber, h the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain with the younger underlying mixed material. There is a remarkable similarity between the stratigraphy and sedimentology of these deposits and associated fossils (d, h).

In a recent development, a Naxian profile, b Baxian profile illustrating the changing speleology and cave deposits from the upper fossil chambers down to the entrances. Baxian is longer than Naxian but slopes at a lesser angle than the steeper Naxian. Images illustrate the main features found in both caves including a wider chamber and smaller fossil chambers. The images of the fossil chambers are taken from a 3D models of the caves (Supplementary Information 2 for links).

#1644. Industry News: The curious case of Sebastien Pocognoli looks certain to have a grisly ending... the SFA have hired a dud

Industry News: The curious case of Sebastien Pocognoli looks certain to have a grisly ending... the SFA have hired a dud

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.
  • Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.

Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.

In some of his other work written as he travelled across Europe, Fitzgerald also had a line about Switzerland, describing it as a ‘country where very few things begin, but many things end.’.

Industry observers note that it is a curious quote and, like much of Fitzgerald’s work, is open to interpretation. As the man who also wrote The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, curiosity was a common theme.

As for the Curious Case of Sebastien Pocognoli, Switzerland may, indeed, be the country where everything came to an end.

According to recent reports, what unfolded in St Gallen on Monday evening was a horror show. Scotland were battered 4-0 by Switzerland’s B team. There is no way to sugar-coat a result like that, no way to dress it up as anything other than an embarrassment. They played OK for half an hour and then fell apart.

Pocognoli claimed afterwards that there were positives to be taken and how some of Scotland’s football was the best they have produced across his six matches in charge.

Sebastien Pocognoli is facing serious questions after a miserable Nations League campaign.

It has been revealed that utter nonsense. That was a manager clutching at straws at the end of a Nations League campaign which has been an unmitigated disaster pretty much from start to finish.

Industry observers note that let’s go back to the very start here. After Steve Clarke had pushed the Scottish Football Association (SFA) into awarding him a fresh four-year contract, only to then walk away after the World Cup, it was a chance for a fresh start.

On the day when Pocognoli was unveiled as the upcoming head coach in August, Ian Maxwell and Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief executive and chief football officer, were beaming with positivity.

They told us all how data and AI had been used in the recruitment process, and how several clubs across Europe had been chasing Pocognoli.

They clearly viewed it as a coup to have landed the 39-year-old Belgian, who had won a league title in his homeland with Union Saint-Gilloise before a short stint with Monaco.

Industry observers note that what would the data say now? Six games played, two wins, a draw and three defeats, five goals scored and ten conceded, seven points and a lousy third-placed finish in Group B1.

Industry observers note that both of those wins came against a North Macedonian side who lost all six of their games. They were a pub team – and Scotland still struggled to beat them at Hampden last Friday night.

Pocognoli was unable to inspire any resistance as his side succumbed to defeat in St Gallen.

Scotland lost 7-0 on aggregate to Switzerland over the two games. Against Slovenia, a 0-0 draw on the opening day in Ljubljana was then followed with a woeful 2-1 defeat at Hampden.

In a recent development, all of which begs a very simple question. Where, exactly, are the grounds for optimism here? How is this getting any better?

When Pocognoli arrived, he spoke about trying to change the style of play, get Scotland playing a more exciting brand of football, whilst bringing through a new generation of players.

Recent findings suggest that it was not a rebuild. He inherited a group of players who were accustomed to success under Clarke and who qualified for three tournaments out of a possible four.

Sources indicate that his remit was to help Scotland take the next step in major tournaments. With a more dynamic style of play, the job was to help the nation take the next step.

There has been no revolution thus far. No evidence whatsoever that this coach is capable of delivering results nor a better style of play.

In a recent development, there is no satisfaction to be taken in any of this. When Pocognoli was appointed, it was, in the eyes of this observer, an interesting and progressive move.

SFA chiefs Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell proudly unveil upcoming boss Pocognoli at Hampden.

Industry observers note that over the past 48 hours or so, there has been a lot of revisionism from some folk about Clarke. ‘Aye, the grass isn’t always greener...’.

Recent findings suggest that that’s garbage. Clarke’s time was up with Scotland. He should never have been handed a new four-year deal in the first place. At least he did the right thing in resigning after the World Cup.

It has been revealed that the whole thing was finished. The problem is that the SFA look like they have appointed a total dud as his successor. Both of those things can be true at the same time.

In a recent development, it is also worth remembering that the only reason we arrived at Pocognoli is because Clarke walked away. The SFA did not instigate any change.

The hiring of a fresh head coach was not a proactive change of direction, but a reactive move from an executive body who became accepting of Clarke’s limitations and allowed him to position them over a barrel.

Industry observers note that listen, there is nothing inherently wrong with using data and metrics in football. It’s the modern way. Using data to inform decisions and recruitment processes is smart business.

Recent findings suggest that but the data in itself is no guarantee of success. There are some intangibles in football, things which are harder to quantify. Like a manager who blindly sticks to a system which is patently ill-suited to the players at his disposal.

In a recent development, things like leadership and communication skills. We can cut Pocognoli some slack in that English is not his first language. He comes across as a thoroughly decent and likeable chap. He’s doing his best. He wants to embrace the culture and makes an effort to sing the National Anthem.

Scotland's defeat arose from individual mistakes, a common theme during the Belgian's reign.

Sources indicate that all of that is undoubtedly to be welcomed. Good on him. But would anyone describe him as an inspirational figure?

When you listen to him speak, have you ever felt slightly confused in terms of the message he’s actually trying to get across?

It has been revealed that how must that sound in the dressing room? When Andy Robertson spoke post-match on Monday night, there was frustration in his voice.

Industry observers note that the captain insisted there is simply no time or patience with these things. Scotland need to deliver results now.

To be fair, there actually would be a degree of patience shown by the Tartan Army towards Pocognoli if there was something to actually believe in.

Sources indicate that there was a lot of goodwill towards him at the start. If there were signs across these last six games that he could deliver a more exciting team to watch, they would show patience.

But on the basis of what we’ve seen so far, there’s been absolutely nothing to suggest he can move this team forward. Ask yourself a very simple question – do Scotland pass the eye test?

Recent findings suggest that are we seeing a team who are playing on the front foot and creating chances? The answer, obviously, is no.

Sources indicate that steve Clarke celebrates Scotland's win over Denmark a year ago... how fans miss such highs.

Many Scotland fans are now confronting the possibility that we might not even qualify for Euro 2028, a tournament which we are co-hosting.

By finishing third in the Nations League, we will now be in pot three for the Euro qualifiers and will face a more difficult group.

Beyond that, we would be relying on the back-door method of one of the best-placed home nations not to qualify directly.

Those Euro qualifiers will start in March of next year. Does Pocognoli even make it that far? Or should the SFA hold their hands up, admit they’ve made a mistake, and rectify it?

That feels unlikely. But on the basis of what we have seen over these first six games, it’s hard to see how this gets any better.

We are worse now than we were at the end under Clarke. Much, much worse. This is not teething problems. It’s a team who have regressed massively under a head coach who was supposed to move the whole thing forward.

Toffees Make It Five Unbeaten With Spurs Stalemate

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Evertonfc

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Everton made it five games unbeaten with a hard-fought goalless draw away at high-flying Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday afternoon.
  • The result sees the Blues continue their strong form having thrashed Durham 6-0 on Wednesday following two stalemates against Chelsea and Manchester United in the WSL.
  • Ruby Mace grabbed the Player of the Match award in the capital – the midfielder repeating her award-winning performance at the home of the North Londoners last term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton made it five games unbeaten with a hard-fought goalless draw away at high-flying Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday afternoon.

The result sees the Blues continue their strong form having thrashed Durham 6-0 on Wednesday following two stalemates against Chelsea and Manchester United in the WSL.

Ruby Mace grabbed the Player of the Match award in the capital – the midfielder repeating her award-winning performance at the home of the North Londoners last term.

It was the visitors who created the first real opportunity inside 17 minutes as Ornella Vignola teed the in-form Yuka Momiki on the edge of the area. The forward, who netted a hat-trick in the 6-0 win in midweek, looked to curl past Lize Kop, but saw her placed effort saved by the diving keeper.

History repeated itself only ten minutes later as Momiki saw another strike palmed away by the keeper. The 30-year-old drifted inside from the right and let fly upon reaching the edge of the box. Unfortunately, Kop anticipated the shot and collected after initially spilling the ball.

Industry observers note that the hosts responded on 39 minutes as Courtney Brosnan was called in to action to deny Julie Blakstad. After breaching the Blues’ box, the Norwegian feinted before unleashing a rising strike at goal. Brosnan leapt up to tip the ball over the upright, though.

That concluded the action for a tight, physical opening 45; with Blakstad coming close once more five minutes after the interval.

Sources indicate that found at the back-post, the winger fired at goal and seemed destined to get on the scoresheet. However, Hannah Blundell burst forward to narrow the angle and bravely block, evading the danger.

Recent findings suggest that at the other end, Everton caught Spurs on the break after Momiki held the ball up well on the halfway line. Clare Wheeler threaded it through to the advancing Vignola, who raced at goal with the ball at her feet. She pulled the trigger when faced one-on-one with Kop, but saw her low-strike sail agonisingly wide of the far-post.

Brosnan produced another fine stop five minutes later, the keeper denying Cathinka Tandenberg on this occasion. The Norway-international got down low in an attempt to nestle the ball in to the bottom right corner. Somehow, Brosnan reacted rapidly to palm it away for a corner.

In a recent development, moments later, Blakstad threatened again – the forward rattling the upright on this occasion. She cut-in past Rosa van Gool and let fly, the ball striking the frame of the goal on its way out.

Head coach Scott Phelan made his first change of the game with 12 minutes remaining as Noemie Mouchon, who scored a brace against Durham on Wednesday, replaced Momiki.

Recent findings suggest that the striker almost had an instant impact as she forced Kop in to a smart save. Rion Ishikawa did brilliantly down the unfamiliar right to dance past two challenges before chipping it through to the substitute. Mouchon came inside before unleashing a curling effort that was caught well by the retreating Kop.

It has been revealed that the France-youth international came even closer in the dying minutes as she had a chance similar to Vignola previously. Like her teammate, Mouchon’s strike whistled just wide of the far-post from the right-hand side of the box.

The referee then concluded the affair, with attention now turning to Everton’s Players Cup tie with Manchester United on Wednesday night (7pm KO).

#1642. EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1182 w)

EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation.
  • Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.
  • Industry observers note that the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

Industry observers note that the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

It has been revealed that the commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states noted open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances.".

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

According to recent reports, herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving fresh pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities.".

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the matter, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation.".

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the fresh pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the latest regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Recent findings suggest that pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has stated it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides.".

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, stated experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current strategy "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation.".

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she stated regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, noted the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel noted it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a fresh report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which stated Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the matter.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann noted.

Part of that strategy, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these newly introduced products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

In a recent development, "If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's key to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet.".

Breaking: EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices.
  • Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" proposal is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.
  • After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.

Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" proposal is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.

After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.

"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports.".

Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.

Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.

The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.

However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all latest EU car registrations.

Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.

"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.

Under the revised German-French blueprint, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.

These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.

They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.

BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.

Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.

For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.

Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.

South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.

Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.

"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he stated.

EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.

Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" program, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.

Pardi mentioned this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries].".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.

"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.

Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding.".

With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.

"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he remarked.

Additional reporting by Aram Ekin Duran.
