Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 47 min read (9496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~47 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing1.
  • According to recent reports, integrated photonic devices have emerged as a powerful platform for the next-generation information technologies, and the development of efficient and scalable integrated photonic circuits has become a central focus of state-of-the-art research.
  • According to recent reports, however, the effectiveness of all-optical devices depends critically on the ability to harness optical nonlinearities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing1. Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses2. Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms3,4,5. However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

According to recent reports, integrated photonic devices have emerged as a powerful platform for the next-generation information technologies, and the development of efficient and scalable integrated photonic circuits has become a central focus of state-of-the-art research. Photonics enables ultrafast signal propagation, low-loss transport, broadband modulation and highly efficient information processing6,7. In this context, it is crucial that the same architecture supports a variety of integrated components, including on-chip coherent light sources, frequency-comb generators, modulators, amplifiers and switches, enabling coherent phase manipulation of propagating optical fields as a key functionality for dynamical reconfigurability and interferometric-based operations.

According to recent reports, however, the effectiveness of all-optical devices depends critically on the ability to harness optical nonlinearities. As conventional platforms based on linear dielectric materials or lithium niobate (LiNbO3) show intrinsically weak nonlinear responses8,9, structures supporting exciton–polaritons have been proposed as an effective alternative. These hybrid light–matter excitations, formed under non-perturbative radiation coupling between excitons and purely photonic eigenmodes, combine photon-like propagation with strong optical nonlinearities, making them attractive for ultrafast all-optical information processing10,11,12,13. Although exciton–polaritons have been extensively studied in vertically confined microcavities, planar architectures such as polariton waveguides14,15,16,17 have recently attracted increasing interest owing to their ability to confine light within smaller modal volumes, thereby enhancing exciton–photon coupling, increasing polariton group velocities and facilitating on-chip integration. When combined with suitable active materials showing large exciton binding energies, polariton operation can be sustained at room temperature5, a condition fulfilled by perovskites, which stand out for their exceptional and tunable optoelectronic properties and ease of processing, eliminating the demanding fabrication procedures typically required for conventional semiconductors. In addition, their strong polariton nonlinearities, comparable to that of gallium arsenide (GaAs)-based systems, makes them an increasingly attractive platform for polariton-based applications at room temperature18,19,20,21. However, fabricating high-quality perovskite photonic components remains challenging because well-defined edges and smooth surfaces are essential for achieving satisfactory performance22,23,24, whereas conventional postprocessing often degrades the crystal morphology and optical quality. Despite recent progress, efficient in-coupling and out-coupling of light remains a main bottleneck. In particular, the realization of coherent on-chip tunable light sources, optical amplification of propagating polariton signals and efficient nonlinear phase control—only partially explored in planar microcavities under cryogenic conditions25 and still absent in guided propagating polariton systems—remains a key outstanding challenge. Overcoming these limitations is crucial to achieving robust, room-temperature, scalable and fully integrated nonlinear photonic devices.

Recent findings suggest that here we address these critical challenges by developing a fully integrated perovskite-based polaritonic circuit in which waveguides and grating couplers are simultaneously defined within the active materials using an innovative bottom-up soft-lithographic strategy that combines surface-tension-assisted and microfluidic growth processes26,27,28. This growth approach eliminates the need for any subsequent postprocessing, enabling the direct integration of hundreds-of-micrometres-long, micrometre-wide caesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) waveguides with subwavelength gratings featuring tunable periodicity and filling factors. Under off-resonant pumping, the integrated gratings provide longitudinal optical feedback, enabling polariton lasing in an in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavity, with emission efficiently propagating along the waveguide and readily tunable by means of the grating geometry. We also demonstrate efficient optical amplification in a two-beam experiment, in which a resonantly injected propagating polariton wavepacket is amplified through stimulation from the exciton reservoir created by an extra off-resonant beam. The threshold-like amplification resembles key features of spiking neurons, offering a promising route towards the development of neuromorphic polariton devices29,30. In parallel, we achieve nonlinear optical phase control of propagating polariton signals, enabling interferometric functionalities with phase shifts reaching 2π. Our results demonstrate room-temperature polaritonic circuits with active nonlinear functionalities, marking an notable step towards ultra-compact, highly nonlinear polariton devices for integrated photonics and optical information processing.

CsPbBr3 perovskite waveguides with various geometries were directly fabricated on glass substrates using a modified soft-lithography approach that combines surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing from a liquid precursor solution, following the procedure sketched in Fig. 1a and detailed in the Methods (Supplementary Figs. 1–4). The process uses a patterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) replica moulded from a silicon master (Fig. 1b), yielding the perovskite waveguides with integrated gratings shown in Fig. 1c–e. This hybrid method enables the direct formation of hierarchical architectures through controlled self-assembly under saturation conditions and controlled temperature, yielding micrometre-scale waveguides decorated with integrated nanometric grating arrays. The soft-lithography route overcomes key limitations of conventional fabrication by exploiting elastomeric replication, enabling a simple, low-temperature and non-destructive process. It eliminates the need for multi-step lithography, avoids postprocessing damages and refractive-index mismatches, while significantly reducing fabrication cost and time.

According to recent reports, a, Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of CsPbBr3 waveguides by means of microfluidic surface-tension-driven lithography. The process follows three main steps: (1) replica moulding in PDMS of the waveguide master (left); (2) capillary-driven distribution of the precursor solution along the microstructured channels under saturated conditions and controlled temperature (centre) and (3) formation of CsPbBr3 microcrystals with the desired morphology and integrated nanometric optical gratings (right). b, Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of representative waveguides with integrated optical gratings fabricated on the silicon master through electron-beam lithography (EBL). c, Confocal images of CsPbBr3 perovskite waveguides with integrated gratings produced by the modified single-step soft-lithography technique described in a. Its features reproduce closely those fabricated in the master. d, SEM image showing a complete grating coupler directly replicated onto the CsPbBr3 perovskite structure. Right inset demonstrates high-resolution view of the grating from the white region in the left panel. e, High-resolution atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurement of a representative grating. f, TE-pol momentum-space photoluminescence map from one of the waveguide gratings. Here β denotes the waveguide momentum, related to the measured outcoupled wavevector by β = k ± 2π/a, where a is the grating pitch. For this specific grating, the pitch was measured to be 240 nm. Two polariton modes (yellow solid lines) are visible and marked as LP0 and LP1, respectively. The two polariton modes arise from strong coupling between two photonic modes (TE0 and TE1, white dashed lines) and the excitonic resonance. Right panel, real-space photoluminescence image of the waveguide in which the emission from several adjacent gratings is visible; the pumping spot is outside from the image in the top part. LP, lower polariton; TE-pol, TE-polarized. Scale bars, 10 μm (b,c,f); 2 μm (d).

It has been revealed that to investigate the optical properties of the fabricated structures, we performed momentum-resolved photoluminescence and reflectivity measurements (Methods). The corresponding maps for both transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) polarizations and different pitches are shown in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. The momentum-resolved photoluminescence, obtained by spatially selecting the emission from one grating, is shown in Fig. 1f for TE polarization. Two strongly coupled modes are clearly visible (yellow solid lines), which we attribute to the fundamental (TE0) and first-order (TE1) lower polariton waveguide modes. Although the upper polariton branch is not visible31,32,33, the characteristic dispersion of the waveguide modes, which is approximated as linear in the weak coupling regime (white dashed lines), reveals an increasing bending approaching the exciton resonance, providing clear evidence of the strong radiation-matter coupling. Reflectivity and photoluminescence data were fitted using a two-coupled-oscillator model yielding Rabi splitting energies of Ω = 140 ± 10 meV for both the TE1 and TE0 modes (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6), consistent with previous reports23,34. The presence of these two modes is compatible with a waveguide thickness ranging between 250 nm and 290 nm, as confirmed by finite-difference time-domain simulations presented in Extended Data Fig. 1 for different grating pitches. It is notable to note that the TE1 mode appears brighter because one of its electric-field maxima lies closer to the top surface of the waveguide, where the grating is patterned, resulting in more efficient coupling to free-space radiation and a larger momentum-space linewidth. The typical real-space photoluminescence emission is shown in the right part of Fig. 1f and the exciton/photon fraction for LPB1 is reported in Supplementary Fig. 8.

In the absence of external optical resonators, lasing in perovskite microstructures can arise from optical feedback provided by sharp crystal facets acting as Fabry–Pérot cavities.23,24,35,36. In waveguide geometries, this feedback occurs predominantly in the transverse direction23, thus proving ineffective for photonic integrated circuits, which normally demand longitudinal propagation. Moreover, this lasing emission lacks spectral tunability, as it is governed by the intrinsic balance between optical gain and loss within the material. Alternative strategies based on isolated perovskite blocks evanescently coupled to active waveguides24 can promote in-plane propagation, but are limited by weak field overlap and inefficient coupling. Longitudinal polariton lasing assisted by integrated grating reflectors was demonstrated in a GaAs-based waveguide at cryogenic temperature17 and in gallium nitride (GaN)-based waveguide at room temperature37. However, in these systems the lasing mode remains confined within the reflective elements, without efficiently coupling into a propagating waveguide mode. By contrast, our approach integrates tunable lasing emission within a guided architecture, providing a direct route towards integrated polaritonic circuits. Moreover, it is achieved through a simple, scalable growth process yielding waveguides with embedded couplers, unlike the more complex fabrication required for GaAs or GaN platforms.

Industry observers note that to verify the formation of such a longitudinal optical feedback, the perovskite waveguide was off-resonantly pumped between two couplers. The real-space TE-polarized photoluminescence maps at excitation powers (P) below (left) and above (right) the lasing threshold (Pth) are shown in Fig. 2a. At low pumping power, the two outcouplers are barely visible, as only a relatively small portion of the emitted light is effectively coupled into the waveguide modes. By contrast, at high excitation power, a pronounced signal emerges from both outcouplers, suggesting that a longitudinal feedback is taking place. Notably, the lasing signal extracted from the grating disappears in TM polarization (Supplementary Fig. 9), confirming the polarization sensitivity of the feedback mechanism. To further investigate the onset and evolution of the lasing emission, we performed a real-space energy-resolved measurement and evaluated the emitted intensity (Extended Data Fig. 2) collected from one of the two outcouplers for the lasing signal (integrated between 2.31 eV and 2.32 eV), as shown in Fig. 2b. A clear threshold is observed at roughly Pth = 55 µJ cm−2, consistent with previous reports on similar perovskite materials19,35,38,39. The transition is accompanied by a clear linewidth narrowing as reported in the inset. The energy-resolved momentum-space maps are shown in Fig. 2c for the below-threshold (left panel) and above-threshold (right panel) regimes, and the corresponding kx–ky maps are reported in Supplementary Fig. 10.

a, Real-space image of a Fabry–Pérot in-plane cavity formed by two gratings (highlighted by the dashed squares); below threshold (left) the emission is dominated by exciton recombination under the pump spot, whereas above threshold (right) the lasing mechanism takes place and the emission from the two gratings is stronger than the photoluminescence not coupled to the guided mode. b, Emitted intensity integrated at the grating position from real-space energy-resolved measurements as a function of pumping fluence. Data points are obtained from three consecutive power-dependence measurements performed on the same structure as shown in blue, green and orange dots. The black points represent the average of the three power-dependence measurements. Dashed black lines are guides for the eye. The inset demonstrates the linewidth below (black line) and above threshold (red line) obtained from energy-resolved momentum-space measurements. c, Corresponding energy-resolved momentum-space emission below (left) and above threshold (right). The white dashed lines indicate the TE0 and TE1 polariton modes propagating downward (dashed lines) and upward (solid line). d, Lasing emission from three different cavities formed by couples of gratings having different pitches (270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, respectively); when the pitch is modified the energy of the lasing energy shifts. Scale bars, 5 μm.

Recent findings suggest that lasing occurs where longitudinal feedback selects a single mode due to the balance between gain and losses taking place at the reflectivity maximum induced by the grating, where losses are minimal. This point38,40 is slightly red-shifted and momentum-shifted with respect to the bandgap because finite-size and thickness variation in the grating profile cause latest loss-favoured grating-to-waveguide backreflections15, as discussed in Supplementary Fig. 11. Lasing modes show a clear blueshift with increasing power, and more Fabry–Pérot modes emerge within the same spectral region (Extended Data Fig. 3). Notably, our configuration does not rely on large reflectivity or a strongly developed stop band; rather, a small but finite reflectivity is sufficient to enable cavity formation and mode selection, owing to the excellent gain properties of CsPbBr3. To demonstrate the spectral tunability of the lasing emission, we have tuned the periodicity within the integrated couplers by keeping their mutual distance constant. As shown in Fig. 2d, for three different grating geometries with pitches of 270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, a progressive blueshift is induced from roughly 2.28 eV to 2.315 eV. The below-threshold and above-threshold dispersions for all the measured gratings are reported in Extended Data Fig. 4. It is important to note that in the present device geometry, longitudinal feedback from the grating couplers coexist with transverse feedback from the waveguide edges. Above-threshold spatially resolved measurements confirm this coexistence, showing a roughly doubled mode spacing for edge emission, consistent with two cavity lengths of roughly 25 μm and 10 μm, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 12). Efficient propagation of the lasing signal along the waveguide allows its collection from the first outcoupler next to the grating-pair cavity element (Extended Data Fig. 6). From these data, together with further resonant propagation measurements, we estimate propagation losses, outcoupler attenuation and optical gain (Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14).

In the following section we demonstrate another key functionality of our system: the optical amplification, which has not been previously achieved in similar polaritonic platforms at room temperature. This is essential for integrated photonic circuits as it compensates for propagation and coupling losses, thus enabling efficient on-chip light transport. We resonantly injected a pulsed beam (signal) through the input grating on the LPB1 mode and monitored the transmitted signal at the output located 25 µm away. A second pulsed beam (amplifier) was off-resonantly exciting the centre of the waveguide between two outcouplers where it generates an incoherent exciton population, as schematically shown in Fig. 3a. The signal beam was kept in the linear regime, thereby avoiding self-phase-modulation effects41 (Supplementary Fig. 15). We recorded the output intensity by scanning the time delay between the two pulses, keeping the signal with a constant intensity and changing the fluence of the amplifier. Figure 3b demonstrates the collected intensity as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, indicated by the blue, orange and green curves, respectively (Methods). At low pump fluences, the output signal remains unchanged, whereas at higher amplifier fluences it is strongly enhanced at 0 delay (Δt = 0 ps) and then decays within roughly 50 ps, demonstrating amplification once a sufficient particle density is reached. The decay follows a single-exponential fit with a characteristic time of 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, more than 1 order of magnitude shorter than the bare photoluminescence decay (Supplementary Fig. 16). To further explain the effect, power-dependent measurements at Δt = 0 ps were performed, as shown in Fig. 3c. Here the bottom panel represents the photoluminescence intensity generated by the off-resonant amplifier alone, which increases quadratically with pump fluence (Supplementary Fig. 17), whereas the top panel corresponds to the intensity measured in the presence of both the signal and the amplifier beams, showing clear amplification with a marked threshold-like behaviour. This trend confirms optical amplification and is consistent with stimulated emission, where the probe stimulates particles from the incoherent exciton reservoir created by the amplifier, possibly assisted by acoustic phonons, recently shown to play a key role in perovskites42. The amplification threshold is found to occur at roughly Pth,Amp = 10 μJ cm−2, that is, well below the lasing threshold.

a, Sketch of the integrated optical circuit used to measure polariton amplification: the off-resonant beam (amplifier) creates an exciton reservoir whereas the resonant beam (signal) excites a polariton state propagating along the waveguide. At the output grating the signal is amplified (amplified signal) thanks to stimulation from the exciton reservoir. Amplifier energy is Eamplifier = 2.58 eV in all the measurements. b, Collected intensity of the amplified signal as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2; black dashed line indicate the exponential fit. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.31 eV. A positive Δt corresponds to the case in which the signal arrives after the non-resonant pump, allowing amplification to take place while the reservoir is present. The decay time, 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, is the average of the exponential-fit values obtained at pump fluences of 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, which yield 22.1 ± 1.4 ps and 18.8 ± 0.9 ps, respectively. c, Power-dependent measurements at time delay 0 ps. Bottom: green dots represent the intensity of the amplifier alone; top, orange dots show the intensity of the amplified signal as a function of the amplifier fluence. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.26 eV. The horizontal error bars represent the power fluctuations of the amplifier, whereas the vertical error bars reflect the standard deviation derived from the signal evaluation across slightly different spectral regions, providing an estimate of the systematic uncertainty. d, Amplification factor as a function of the signal energy for two different amplifier fluences (P1 = 25 μJ cm−2 and P2 = 35 μJ cm−2) as indicated in c by the blue and red dashed lines. The amplification closely follows the photoluminescence spectral profile, increasing with the photoluminescence intensity. The photoluminescence spectrum, shown in arbitrary units, is included for qualitative comparison.

To test the spectral efficiency, we selected two amplifier fluences (P1 and P2, blue and red dashed vertical lines in Fig. 3c), both kept between the amplification and the lasing threshold, and scanned the signal energy, keeping its fluence constant. Figure 3d highlights the amplification factor as a function of the signal energy, defined as \(A=\frac{({S}_{{\rm{out}}}-{A}_{0})}{{S}_{0}}\), where Sout is the total output signal, and A0 and S0 are the independently measured amplifier and signal contributions, respectively. Clear amplification is observed over a broad energy range, with a superlinear dependence on signal energy and increasing spectral efficiency due to more efficient scattering and reduced group velocity, which enhances the interaction time with the reservoir. Crucially, amplification is observed even at energies well outside the narrow spectral region where lasing occurs (Supplementary Fig. 18) thus ruling out a cavity-mode feeding mechanism, which would instead be confined to the narrow spectral region defined by the lasing modes. In Supplementary Fig. 19, we present representative real-space maps of the signal, the amplifier and the amplified signal. Moreover, at the highest signal energy for which propagation is still sustained in the system the amplification factor approaches two orders of magnitude. Taking into account the spatial extension of the reservoir (Supplementary Fig. 18), we estimate the optical gain within a simple one-dimensional model as g = ln(A)/L, where A is the measured amplification factor and L is the effective interaction length, approximated by the amplifier full-width at half-maximum (13–15 µm). This yields values in the range of 5 × 102–3 × 103 cm−1 depending on the signal energy. Moreover, above the lasing threshold, the amplified signal saturates (Extended Data Fig. 7), consistent with reservoir depletion induced by the self-oscillating mode. Combining room-temperature operation with liquid-phase synthesis, our results represent a great advance over GaAs-based or ZnO-based platforms, which instead require cryogenic operation and demanding epitaxial growth16,43. In addition, the strong-coupling regime enables amplification through bosonic stimulation rather than population inversion, allowing operation at lower pump powers than conventional gain media.

We then exploit the complex geometries enabled by our fabrication approach to demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton system. A resonant signal beam (Eres = 2.265 eV) is injected through the input grating, propagates along the structure and is subsequently split into the two arms of an interferometric Y-splitter. At the end of each arm, the waveguide edges act as outcouplers, allowing for the formation of an interference pattern in the momentum space, directly accessing the relative phase difference between the two arms. A non-resonant pulse is then introduced in only one arm of the Y-splitter. A schematic of the configuration is shown in Fig. 4a, and the reflectivity image of the Y-splitter termination and the corresponding outcoupled signal are shown in Fig. 4b. A representative momentum-space map recorded with only the propagating signal shows the expected interference pattern (Fig. 4c), whose origin is confirmed by selectively removing one output from the detection path (Supplementary Fig. 20). We then monitor the interference fringe shift as a function of the phase-shifter pulse energy at zero delay Δt = 0 ps between the optical shifter and the propagating signal beam. As shown in Fig. 4d, where the intensity profile along kx is plotted as a function of the optical-shifter fluence, a pronounced shift is generated. The phase shift, extracted from sinusoidal fits of the interferograms, reaches up to 2π with increasing pump pulse energy (Fig. 4e). As a consistency check, moving the phase-shifter beam to the opposite arm reverses the fringe shift direction (Extended Data Fig. 8), whereas amplification is observed only in the pumped arm (Supplementary Fig. 21). We model the experiment using two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance, as described in the Methods. At fixed probe frequency, this shift produces a change in the polariton wavevector and the corresponding phase accumulated over the propagation length is reported in Fig. 4f as a function of the exciton resonance shift.

In a recent development, a, Schematic of the Y-splitter device with an integrated input grating used to split a propagating resonant signal inside the structure while a non-resonant phase shifter (EPS = 2.58 eV) is applied only on one of its two arms. The ends of the two arms outcouple the propagating signal and behave as spatially separated coherent emitters, generating an interference pattern in momentum space that provides direct access to the relative phase. b, Real-space image of the Y-splitter termination (top) and the corresponding outcoupled signal (bottom) when only the resonant beam is present. c, Representative momentum-space map showing the interference pattern arising from coherent out-coupling of the two arms. d, Evolution of the interference fringes for increasing phase-shifter fluence. The direction of the fringe shift is highlighted by the black arrow. Bottom black profile represents the signal alone. Note that the incident pulse energy per operation is used here as the relevant metric (rather than fluence), as appropriate for single-device operation. The device footprint is roughly 20 μm2. e, Phase shift as a function of energy per pulse, showing a continuous increase reaching 2π. f, Calculated phase shift considering two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance. Scale bars, 2 μm (b), 1.5 μm–1 (c).

Sources indicate that finally, after establishing the presence of a suitable π-phase shift in the Y-splitter geometry, we extend this functionality to a full Mach–Zehnder interferometer. The polariton mode is resonantly excited at 2.265 eV through the input grating, while the transmitted signal is collected at the output, with the phase shifter applied to one arm of the interferometer, as illustrated in Fig. 5a,b. The output intensity is extracted from a fixed spatial region at the grating outcoupler and is shown in Fig. 5c after background subtraction (Supplementary Fig. 22). As the phase-shifter energy increases, the signal evolves from a maximum to a minimum and then back to a maximum, demonstrating a full 2π response well reproduced by a sine-squared fit. Notably, this sizable phase shift is achieved within an ultra-compact guided footprint (roughly 20 µm2, Fig. 5b), compared with millimetre-scale lithium-niobate phase shifters44,45. The large modulation is enabled by the polaritonic nature of the guided mode that enhances the nonlinear response to the pump-induced reservoir. Beyond its compactness, the direct use of polaritonic nonlinearities, with a residual contribution from the excitonic reservoir due to the off-resonant excitation, offers a route towards ultrafast integrated circuitry compared with thermo-optic nonlinearities46,47,48.

a, Microscope image of the Mach–Zehnder interferometer with an integrated input and output grating. b, Example of the experimental configuration adopted: a resonant beam with a full-width at half-maximum comparable to the size of the grating coupler is focused on the input grating (left, signal input), propagates along the structure and is outcoupled at the output grating (right, signal output). The phase-shifter beam was pumping one arm of the interferometer. The images of the signal input, phase shifter and signal output regions were acquired separately and subsequently rescaled in intensity. c, Signal output as a function of the phase-shifter energy: black dots represent the experimental data, and the red line indicates the fitted curve. The data are collected at Δt = 0 ps, corresponding to temporal synchronization between the travelling signal beam and the phase-shifter beam at the phase-shifter spatial position. Scale bars, 10 μm.

Sources indicate that in summary, we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polariton waveguide platform operating at room temperature, combining strong nonlinear propagation, tunable polariton lasing, optical amplification and nonlinear phase control within a single device. Our approach introduces a hybrid and high-throughput soft-lithography method that combines surface-tension–guided assembly with microfluidics, enabling single-step direct fabrication of active waveguides with integrated grating couplers. This provides a straightforward, cost-effective and scalable route for realizing self-assembled complex polaritonic architectures without the need for specialized vacuum equipment or epitaxial reactors. The developed architecture supports on-chip polariton lasing, with wavelength-selective emission enabled by longitudinal feedback from the integrated gratings and efficient propagation along the waveguide. Beyond lasing, we demonstrate room-temperature amplification of guided polariton signals by nearly two orders of magnitude. The threshold-like amplification and nonlinear response suggest potential for neuromorphic polariton devices, in which tailored excitation geometries and pulse sequences could enable neuron-like operations such as signal integration and threshold-triggered emission.

Furthermore, we demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton configuration, achieving phase shifts exceeding π within an ultra-compact footprint. Crucially, we harness this capability in a fully integrated Mach–Zehnder interferometer, enabling direct conversion of phase modulation into intensity modulation. The ability to coherently control the phase of propagating signals, combined with intrinsic ultrafast polaritonic nonlinearities, establishes this platform as a promising route towards ultrafast on-chip interferometric devices. These features—combining room-temperature operation, material tunability, scalable and cost-effective fabrication, and rich nonlinear functionalities—establish perovskite polariton waveguides as a versatile and promising platform for next-generation integrated photonic and polaritonic technologies.

According to recent reports, the grating and waveguide nanostructures and microstructures were fabricated on 25 × 25 mm Si(100) substrates using EBL (RAITH Voyager) followed by reactive ion etching. The grating pattern was defined using a 130-nm-thick poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) electron-beam resist layer spin-coated onto the silicon substrate and exposed by EBL at a dose of 580 μC cm−2. The exposed resist was developed in a MIBK:IPA (1:3) solution. A 40-nm-thick chromium film, serving as an etch hard mask, was subsequently deposited by electron-beam evaporation, and the remaining resist was removed in acetone. The pattern was transferred for 50 nm into the silicon substrate using fluorine-based reactive ion etching (CF4, CHF3, O2, Ar). The chromium mask was then removed by wet chemical etching. An analogous process was used for the fabrication of the waveguide structures, with optimized parameters as follows: PMMA resist thickness of 360 nm, EBL exposure dose of 280 μC cm−2, chromium mask thickness of 60 nm and reactive ion etching etching depth of 250 nm. Following chromium mask removal, the silicon master was cleaned in a piranha solution for 15 min to eliminate any residual organic contamination. The final silicon master featured microwire waveguides and interferometer-like geometries with lateral dimensions from 2 µm to 30 µm, and a height of 250 nm. Each waveguide incorporated nanometre-scale grating arrays covering areas of roughly 10 × 10 µm2, with a height of 50 nm, pitches between 240 nm and 300 nm and varying filling factors, directly etched onto the surface. The aspect ratios (height/width) of the patterned structures, including both the waveguides and the gratings, ranged from approximately 0.01 to 0.60. The grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4), so that the grating lines remain confined within the inner region of the waveguide and do not overlap with the waveguide borders in the etch mask, thereby avoiding local sidewall indentations during the two-step dry-etching process and preserving a more uniform waveguide geometry for crystal growth. For the interferometer, the structure includes a sequence of lateral modulations before the Y-splitter, efficiently redistributing the guided mode into the two branches (Supplementary Fig. 4).

According to recent reports, perovskite devices were fabricated using a modified soft-lithography approach that combined surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing of a liquid precursor solution, using PDMS replicas moulded from silicon masters with predefined multiscale geometries. A mixture of PDMS prepolymer and curing agent (10:1, Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was cast onto the Si master and cured at 140 °C for 10 min. The polymerized PDMS layer was then carefully detached from the master before the use. A 0.42 M precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 106 mg of CsBr and 183.5 mg of PbBr2 (1:1 molar ratio) in 1.2 ml of dimethylsulfoxide. The mixture was stirred at 80 °C on a hotplate inside a nitrogen-filled glove box for 2 h, yielding a clear solution. Immediately before use, the precursor solution was diluted to concentrations in the range 0.05–0.1 M for the CsPbBr3 crystal growth. The precursor solution was deposited in contact with the patterned PDMS replica until the capillary pressure required for complete imbibition of the microstructures and nanostructures was reached. Once nucleation began, with the liquid meniscus pinned to the sidewalls of the nanoscale features, the PDMS replica was placed in conformal contact with a glass substrate to seal the microwire waveguides26,27. At this stage, capillary forces and surface interactions guided the solution through the microfluidic channels. Within the confined geometry, the reduced precursor volume and the progressively increasing concentration and viscosity gradients promoted perovskite nucleation through surface-tension-driven self-assembly precisely at the elastomer–air interface of each microstructure and nanostructure28,49,50,51. Crystallization inside the microchannels was optimized by imposing controlled temperature ramps (from 4 °C to room temperature) and by maintaining controlled vapour saturation and a pressure of 0.02 N cm−2 (refs. 52,53). After complete solvent evaporation, the PDMS replica was removed, yielding CsPbBr3 positive structures directly on the glass substrate that faithfully reproduced the microscale and nanoscale features of the original Si master. To assess fabrication reproducibility, we report in Supplementary Fig. 23 a set of nominally identical microwire arrays fabricated under the same conditions. The samples highlighted a consistent optical response, with only minor detuning variations. It is crucial to note that the grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width, see Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4, to preserve continuous sidewalls in the elastomeric microchannels used for soft-lithography growth, ensuring uniform capillary filling and crystallization conditions while avoiding sidewall discontinuities that could introduce structural defects or make the crystal more fragile during replica peeling. The accessible limits of the proposed fabrication approach were determined by the fidelity of pattern transfer from the master mould to the elastomeric replica and subsequently to the perovskite crystal. On the basis of the aspect ratios demonstrated here (0.01–0.6), we anticipate that perovskite waveguides with thicknesses of roughly 100–150 nm and lateral dimensions of roughly 250–400 nm should be feasible. For periodic nanostructures, we note that some of the geometries investigated in this work (Supplementary Fig. 2) already contain lateral features as small as 50–80 nm, approaching the practical resolution limit of standard PDMS-based replication. Further reduction of the feature size would probably require optimization of the elastomeric replica itself.

It has been revealed that confocal images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope in high-resolution mode (1,024 × 1,024 pixel). Samples were prepared on microscope slides and characterized using a 488-nm excitation laser and a main beam splitter (MBS 488/639-nm) with appropriate photomultiplier tube (PMT) and gallium arsenide phosphide (GaAsP) detectors. All samples were imaged at various magnifications using Plan-Apochromat objectives of ×10 with a numerical aperture of NA = 0.45, ×20 NA = 0.8 and ×40 NA = 0.95. Three-dimensional images were obtained using the Z-stack scanning mode, which generated optical slices at various depths. Image analysis across different acquisition channels, tomographic reconstructions, spectral profiles and three-dimensional rendering were performed using the dedicated ZEN BLUE software.

Recent findings suggest that AFM measurements were performed with a Dimension Icon (Bruker AXS) instrument, equipped with the Nanoscope V controller. Images were acquired in air, at room temperature, in Tapping Mode to protect the samples from damage. A rotated tapping etched silicon probe (Bruker) with a nominal radius of curvature R ≤ 8 nm was used. The morphology of the Si masters was investigated using a Sigma 300 (Zeiss) field emission SEM operated at an acceleration voltage of 5 kV and with an in-lens detector.

All the optical measurements were performed by using microscope objectives at ×100 magnification and a numerical aperture of 0.9 (Zeiss) in a reflection configuration. The pumping lasers were taken from a pulsed source (Pharos, Light Conversion) with a tunable repetition rate and a pulse duration of <290 fs, which drove two computer-controlled optical parametric amplifier (OPA) stages (Orpheus OPA, Light Conversion). The OPA outputs were independently tunable in wavelength and, depending on the specific measurement (single-beam or double-beam excitation), were used either simultaneously or individually. In all the experiments, the repetition rate was set to 10 kHz. Energy-resolved momentum-space maps were collected by imaging the back focal plane of the objective onto the entrance of a spectrometer (Andor, Kymera 328i Spectrograph), equipped with three gratings (150 lines per mm, 300 lines per mm, 600 lines per mm) and coupled to a two-dimensional charge-coupled device (CCD camera, Andor, iStar 334T). For photoluminescence off the resonance pump, the laser was set to 480 nm and the emitted photoluminescence signal was filtered using an edgepass filter (Thorlabs, FELH0500) to suppress the residual excitation laser and isolate the emission. TE and TM polarizations were defined with the waveguide axis aligned to the entrance slits of the spectrometer, such that the electric field was parallel (TE) or perpendicular (TM) to the grating periodicity. The two polarizations were selectively monitored by using a half-wave plate (AHWP10M-600) and a linear polarizer (GTH10M-A) along the detection line. The laser pumping power was controlled by using a variable neutral-density wheel filter. For double-beam experiments, the two OPA outputs were temporally matched by using a delay line (Newport, M-ILS 150CC DC Servo Linear Stage). Reflectivity measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 5 were performed by using a broadband white-light illumination in a reflection configuration, with a spot diameter of roughly 10 μm on the grating coupler. For the photoluminescence measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 7, the waveguide was excited between two gratings whereas for Supplementary Fig. 6 the emission from a single grating was spatially selected. With reference to Fig. 3b, the temporal profiles were obtained by subtracting the residual photoluminescence signal generated by the amplifier alone, which remained constant across all temporal scans. The amplifier-only signal was collected separately using the same exposure time and then subtracted from the measurements in which both beams were simultaneously present. The same procedure was applied to the measurements in Fig. 4c,d, for which the signal obtained with the phase shifter alone was recorded under identical conditions and subtracted from the corresponding datasets. For the amplification measurements, Δt = 0 ps is defined as the relative amplifier-signal delay that maximizes the amplified signal intensity at the pumped region. This delay was experimentally optimized at each amplifier power, thereby inherently accounting for the relaxation dynamics leading to the population responsible for amplification and their possible dependence on the amplifier power.

To quantitatively relate the measured phase difference to a microscopic excitonic energy shift, we consider two waveguides governed by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one of them subjected to a small blueshift of the exciton resonance. (c-e) Energy resolved real space emission maps along the direction indicated in a, b for three different pumping fluences: 35 μJ cm−2 (c), 53 μJ cm−2 (d) and 70 μJ cm−2 (e). a) Normalized emission spectra measured below (green) and above (orange) the polariton lasing threshold, highlighting the spectral region in which the lasing modes emerge. b) Normalized emission spectra measured at increasing excitation fluence, showing the evolution of the two lasing modes (Mode 1 and Mode 2). Spectra are vertically offset for clarity. The first visible lasing mode blueshifts upon increasing the pumping fluence and a second lasing mode appears, still located within the grating-induced reflectivity region. c) Emission energy of Mode 1 (blue) and Mode 2 (orange) as a function of excitation fluence, showing a blueshifts of 3.4 meV and 1.9 meV, respectively. Industry observers note that a) Real-space PL map collected below- (bottom panel) and above (top panel) the lasing threshold. The two gratings on the left side were pumped in between thus forming the cavity unit responsible for lasing emission. The lasing signal then efficiently propagate along the waveguide axis and is partially outcoupled by the nearest outcoupler. b) Real space intensity profiles below (blue line) and above (orange line) the lasing threshold. Note that the first outcoupler next to the grating-pair cavity element is well visible confirming efficient and long-range propagation of the lasing mode along the waveguide. For this specific structure the pitch is 270 nm, the lasing energy appears at 2,283 meV and propagates at an exciton fraction of around X = 0.4. Below threshold power is around 30 μJ cm−2 while above threshold is around 100 μJ cm−2.

Amplification factor as a function of the amplifier fluence for three different energies of the resonant propagating signal: 2,235 meV (green), 2,255 meV (orange), and 2,290 meV (blue) respectively. Once the system starts to lase by itself (red region in the right part), the intensity of the seeded amplified signal tends to saturate. The saturation can be understood considering that the self-oscillating mode represents a competition channel for the reservoir depletion.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea.
  • Merz draws on Germany's own reunification experience, saying division causes suffering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These updates have been closed.

Below, you can review the leading headlines from and about Germany from Friday, October 30:.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea.

Merz draws on Germany's own reunification experience, saying division causes suffering.

Two German leaders, two parallel missions across Asia.

While President Frank-Walter Steinmeier sought to reinforce ties with China in Beijing, Chancellor Friedrich Merz toured Japan, South Korea and Singapore, promoting closer cooperation among what he calls the world's "middle powers.".

Together, the visits highlight Berlin's effort to lower risks without decoupling from China.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany's annual inflation rate eased to 2.8% in October from 3.3% in September, with economists pointing to the government's fuel tax cut as the main reason.

Preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office highlighted energy prices rose 12.2% compared with a year earlier, down from 14.9% in September. Services inflation slowed to 2.5%, while food inflation remained at 0.4%.

It has been revealed that "The decisive factor was the fuel tax cut," said Silke Tober of the Macroeconomic Policy Institute. The reduction took effect in October and runs through December, although rising crude oil prices partly offset the savings at the pump.

It has been revealed that ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski mentioned higher energy costs had yet to feed through into broader price increases. Unlike during the 2022 energy crisis, consumers were unwilling or unable to absorb substantially higher prices, he said.

In a recent development, but economists warned the relief could prove temporary. "Gas and oil prices have risen significantly again in recent weeks," stated Stephanie Schoenwald, an economist at Germany's state-owned development bank KfW, citing continuing conflicts and lower inventories.

It has been revealed that german President's Frank-Walter Steinmeier latest trip to Asia was intended to provide more clarity. Amid a delicate period, Steinmeier sought a balancing act in China between respect and criticism.

In a recent development, it was a state visit of a kind rarely seen today. For four days, Steinmeier traveled across the country: from Hefei, where the German automaker Volkswagen's China operations are headquartered, through historic villages and the imposing landscapes of the Yellow Mountains. He also visited several points of interest of Chinese history, art, and science, and finally, he headed to Tiananmen Square in the heart of Beijing's political center.

According to recent reports, steinmeier—who is set to leave office in March 2027— spoke as a statesman and diplomat on matters of German and European interest. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Steinmeier have known each other for many years, so in this respect, the president was the right man to address even the most difficult issues as a European.

This political balancing act between respect and criticism did not trigger any visible outrage in Beijing.

When he spoke with Chinese leaders about their subsidies for exports to Europe and the related concern of the trade deficit, Xi replied: "I am ready to work together to open a upcoming chapter in the comprehensive strategic partnership between our two countries and to advance the development of global governance.".

Just how much willingness lies behind the push for a strategic partnership will become clear during further negotiations between the EU and China.

Xi Jinping seems to understand that a persistent trade deficit with Europe could also become a problem for his country, as an economic crisis in Europe could further strain China's economy.

As "the world's second- and third-largest economies," China and Germany also bear "an important responsibility for the development of relations between China and Europe, as well as for stable growth in the global economy," Xi Jinping said. While that may not sound like a breakthrough yet, it certainly sounds like an understanding.

In contrast to his economic arguments, Steinmeier's political appeals for Beijing to assume more responsibility for the international order fell on deaf ears.

The German president addressed global conflicts and wars on several occasions in Beijing, including Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine. But he received no responses in official statements.

That same evening, the news channel of the Chinese TV network CCTV aired a report that merely covered Steinmeier's visit to a well-known astrophysics institute.

There was no mention of the call for China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, to do more to promote world peace.

Mitat Özdemir is one of more than 870,000 Turkish workers who were recruited to Germany by a government program between 1961 and 1973. He dealt with tough factory work, language barriers and cultural differences.

According to recent reports, six decades later, he and his family still live in Germany. How did the program from back then shape their lives and modern Germany?

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.

North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.

"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.

"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he remarked, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.

North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state.".

A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.

The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.

The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.

The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.

Munich police mentioned the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories.".

The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.

The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.

In a recent development, german politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, profits of German luxury car brand Audi for the third quarter came plunged 87% year-on-year to €95 million ($106 million), the Volkswagen subsidiary reported on Friday. This is a drop from €718 million seen in the same quarter last year.

The drop comes amid weak demand in China, and US tariffs.

"Market and competitive conditions have become significantly more difficult in the third quarter," Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger told journalists on a call.

A ban on newly introduced Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.

Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.

Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.

"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.

The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.

The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.

When the entertaining but ultimately rather pointless Ralf Rangnick was tasked with holding the fort as manager at Manchester United five years ago, he was asked whether his much-admired style of football – the high-intensity gegenpress aped by disciples such as Jurgen Klopp – could work with a team that had Cristiano Ronaldo, 36, and Edinson Cavani, 34, in it.

It is this kind of strange, blinkered hubris that we should not expect Mauricio Pochettino to bring with him to Old Trafford.

According to recent reports, heaven knows we have seen enough of that in recent times. Ruben Amorim and his back three. Erik ten Hag and… well maybe one day we will understand what all that was supposed to be about.

It has been revealed that but no, this will not be Pochettino. This cannot be Pochettino.

It has been revealed that this United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football. This is not Tottenham Hotspur 2016. It is not Kyle Walker, Toby Alderweireld, Son Heung-min and Harry Kane. It is not physical and youthful and energetic.

According to recent reports, mauricio Pochettino is waving goodbye to the US national team and hello to Man United this week. But he faces a daunting task at Old Trafford.

This United squad is not one built for the latest United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football.

That is why Pochettino’s battle – at least for the remainder of this season – will be about hearts and minds as much as it is about anything revolutionary that he can bring to bear on the training fields of Carrington.

Recent findings suggest that the good news for those hoping for quick improvement is that Pochettino – at least the one who took Spurs to a Champions League final in 2019 and to within a sniff of a Premier League title a few years earlier – is adept at the mental and emotional side of football. It is upon this that, initially at least, he may wish to rely.

Son told me about this when we sat down to look back on his career in England. He was prolific under Pochettino, a scorer of 75 goals in four-and-a-half seasons under the Argentine. But it was not always like that. Once – just like several current players at United – he was disaffected and unhappy.

‘Mauricio turned me round and it wasn’t about football,’ Son told me. ‘It was about me as a person and how he made he feel.

Sources indicate that ‘I needed help, basically. And he gave me it.

According to recent reports, 'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words. It was unbelievable.

‘Sometimes he had been my coach and sometimes he had been like my family.’.

Pochettino inherits a jigsaw puzzle with the wrong-shaped pieces at Old Trafford. It’s a squad put together for and by six different managers.

Pochettino will want to improve the fitness levels at United and his intense methods might feel like an ice bath to their players.

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words,' states Son Heung-min of his manager at Tottenham. 'It was unbelievable... sometimes he was like my family’.

In a recent development, but the likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Amad Diallo simply could not maintain that level of exertion once the surge in adrenaline had spiked. By the time the game reached the hour mark, United were 4-2 down.

It is certain Pochettino will wish to improve some levels of fitness at United and his methods will perhaps feel like an ice bath to some of those United players who have approached the basic prerequisite of running like some kind of optional extra at times this season.

Sources indicate that at Spurs, players were occasionally known to vomit during training. Pochettino told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

According to recent reports, six or seven years later at Chelsea, meanwhile, he punished striker Nicolas Jackson for picking up five largely needless yellow cards by ordering him to run laps of the training pitch. Jackson was only told why it was happening as he lay on the grass in a heap afterwards.

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa whose ‘Murderball’ sessions eventually arrived in England during his spell at Leeds United eight years ago. The stated aim is simple.

‘With Mauricio, there is no hiding,’ noted former Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana on the Rest Is Football podcast.

‘Everything is high-intensity, pressing from the front, and repeating sprints again and again in training so that it becomes automatic on a Saturday.’.

According to recent reports, trawl through Pochettino’s time as a frontline coach and the testimonies of unstinting, high-intensity work are strikingly similar. There has been no great change in the belief, even when he arrived in America to coach the US national team ahead of this summer’s World Cup.

'He brings that club intensity into the national team environment,’ notes Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie. ‘You immediately feel the tempo he expects.’.

Recent findings suggest that for this to work well, a coach needs two things. A pre-season in which to embed that specific kind of fitness and a squad assembled to play that way.

At United, Pochettino has neither so we can expect it to be a slow burn. He is approaching the busiest period of the playing schedule – his team will play 12 games in the next six and a half weeks – and has immobile central defenders, full backs with limitations and a midfield unit that lacks legs when compared to the best in the Premier League and Europe.

Equally, Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new. Ten years ago, it was Klopp’s Liverpool. Now it’s Fabian Hurzeler’s Brighton and many, many others.

Every player has a brain and a mind, though, and it is here that Pochettino will in all likelihood seek to make the greatest gains ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and beyond.

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

It has been revealed that there is not a United manager since the end of the Sir Alex Ferguson era who has not run into trouble with individual players at some point. Ten Hag with Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho and Raphael Varane. Amorim with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo. Carrick with his captain, Fernandes.

According to recent reports, this, as much as anything, is what has held United back this season. United do not have a squad fit to win the league but that it sits in the bottom three notes everything for the way Carrick and his coaching staff failed at their side of the deal.

According to recent reports, pochettino’s friendship with Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment. Indeed, there are similarities to be found between the two. Pochettino, for example, is a small details man, a coach who understands that mood and motivation and cohesion can be just as crucial as tactics or indeed anything the opposition can bring on a Saturday afternoon.

Having reached out yesterday to a former Southampton player for input on his ex-manager’s methods, the former international gave an insight – albeit unwittingly – into the kind of loyalty Pochettino can inspire.

‘We need to let him integrate at United his own way,’ came the reply. ‘I don’t think he needs us talking about his secrets.’.

Sources indicate that pochettino can be blunt with players. He was with Son. He was with Kane.

‘He mentioned, “You need to do this and this and that’s why you’re not in the squad”,’ Kane once told Daily Mail Sport. ‘And it just hit me. This is what I’ve got to do.’.

Sources indicate that equally, the 54-year-old trades in subtlety. At Tottenham, he would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in. He had staff video them at training and wondered why they always looked happier when they walked off at the end.

Pochettino’s friendship with Sir Alex Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment.

According to recent reports, as strange as it sounds, Pochettino chose the detergent in the washing room as he believed the smell of the first team kit was important. He dropped a player simply because he had noticed him eating stodgy food before sessions and another because he believed his choice of car to be inappropriate to his relative lowly standing in the game.

Recent findings suggest that these are the kinds of things that look clever when you win and like upcoming-age bunkum when you don’t. At Spurs, Pochettino’s results spoke for him but what is critical now is what version has walked through the door at Old Trafford.

It’s true that, to a large extent, we all view him as Pochettino 2016. In the decade that has followed, there have been underwhelming spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. His attempts at making the kind of emotional connections he thrives on in Paris, for example, soon ran into a brick wall with the words ‘Neymar’ and ‘Mbappe’ written on it.

To return to the Ferguson link again, Pochettino has not previously been shy of perceived similarities.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Ferguson used to tell his players that working hard is a talent,’ he wrote in his 2017 book Brave Upcoming World. ‘To me, if a player doesn’t work hard for the team, he won't play. Nothing happens by chance.’.

Sources indicate that what manager in football doesn’t value basic endeavour? Not one but, as mutual trust and shared belief starts to wane during a run of bad results, even the basics can get lost. With this in mind and with Pochettino’s energy and charisma in the building, it’s not unrealistic to expect a upcoming manager bounce at Old Trafford.

His relationship with Fernandes will be crucial and the Portuguese should not expect the captaincy to be a given. At Tottenham, Pochettino gave it to his goalkeeper, Hugo Lloris.

Pochettino knows that coaches can’t speak to players the way they used to, or indeed may wish to. A greater degree of emotional intelligence is required.

Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez - both publicly critical of the set-up at United this season - can expect private words of advice from their new boss.

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford a wiser manager for working amid the background noise at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea.

Recent findings suggest that united’s players can therefore expect WhatsApp messages at 11pm at night – sometimes including attachments of training clips – quiet words of advice or observation when passing their manager in a corridor or even a short note, serious or otherwise, left in a dressing room locker. How the likes of Fernandes, Cunha, Rashford, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez respond to all this will be key.

So, too, will Pochettino’s ability or otherwise to make the best of the clunky chain of executive command that sits above him. At Tottenham, Pochettino and chairman Daniel Levy hit a sweet spot that wasn’t to last but for a time saw them so in tune they even took a horse-riding trip together. It was a synchronicity that electrified the whole football club.

Here in Manchester in 2026-27, it will feel different. At United, senior players criticise executives to the media while the fans wave green-and-gold scarves on matchday and sing unpleasant songs about not one but two different ownership groups. None of that will go away just because yet another manager is through the door.

It has been revealed that pochettino may feel he has some experience of such background noise from his time at PSG and indeed Chelsea. Equally, much of what happens over the course of the rest of this season and, if he is lucky, beyond will depend on his own reserves of energy, desire and self-regeneration. Does his own well remain deep enough?

The man who swept into Southampton with little-to-no English but bags of ideas and energy in January 2013 was an irresistible force of nature and he ran hot through the Premier League for a while. If he brings some of that to Old Trafford then he has a chance of making an impression at least.

According to recent reports, but Pochettino’s take on Murderball, punishment laps and the infamous ‘Gacon’ 5km running drill he has been known to use may have to wait until the summer. United’s immediate challenges, he will find, are more about a failing culture, centring less on playing style and more on emotional substance.

Breaking: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
  • "People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW.
  • Recent findings suggest that the jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it.".

Recent findings suggest that the jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity.".

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, highlights how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

It has been revealed that names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer stated their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages.".

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

In a recent development, "Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Recent findings suggest that even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on.".

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

Industry observers note that "People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'".

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

It has been revealed that tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to.".

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions.".

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'".

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point.".

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

Recent findings suggest that "I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there.".

Recent findings suggest that but Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it.".

Industry observers note that that does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered.".

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny.".
