  • Mauricio Pochettino received a near-perfect sendoff as US men's national team head coach on Tuesday in Cincinnati, where Manchester United's next manager watched his now-former players beat Haiti before bidding an emotional farewell to his adopted country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By ALEX RASKIN, US SPORTS NEWS EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 21:06 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 00:56 EST, 18 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino received a near-perfect sendoff as US men's national team head coach on Tuesday in Cincinnati, where Manchester United's next manager watched his now-former players beat Haiti before bidding an emotional farewell to his adopted country.

Christian Pulisic, Pochettino's brightest pupil over the last two seasons, rose to the occasion by scoring on a gravity-defying bicycle kick in the 25th minute and 18-year-old prospect Julian Hall followed in the 43rd with a goal of his own.

But for all of the excitement on the field – where Pochettino helped rebuild the American attack with a high-intensity style – all eyes were on the manager as he embraced his team one last time.

Recent findings suggest that with the 2-0 win (8-0 aggregate), the USMNT now advances to the CONCACAF Nations League semifinals, but that's no longer Pochettino's concern. Instead, former American fullback and current under-23 manager Steve Cherundolo is expected to take over on an interim basis, while Pochettino turns his attention to an 18th-place United squad that has just one win in the English Premier League through 10 matches this season.

'When you finish the game, you start in your mind to think about different things,' Pochettino noted after the win. 'Of course, it's tough because it's emotional. Because I really love these guys, and I love the players. I love the staff. I love the fans and everything.'.

Following the win, Pochettino was scheduled to fly from northern Kentucky to Manchester aboard a private plane chartered by his latest club. The quick escape offered the chance to avoid major airlines following Friday's chaotic nationwide shutdown, and perhaps a few hours' sleep for a 54-year-old starting his new job on Wednesday at Carrington Training Centre.

Pochettino spent two years with the USMNT, helping to rebuild an attack around Pulisic.

Pochettino hugs a staff member prior to the CONCACAF Nations League Quarterfinal match.

Pochettino paces along a near-empty sideline after much of his staff left for Manchester.

And Pochettino didn't proposal on traveling alone.

Outgoing USMNT first-team coach Miguel D'Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott were expected to join Pochettino aboard the flight to Manchester, where assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez as well as Pochettino's son and fitness coach Sebastiano have already begun preparing for Sunday's matchup with Liverpool at Anfield.

The quick turnaround means Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty. Furthermore, he is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference around lunchtime on Friday.

The Argentine national is replacing Michael Carrick at Old Trafford on a two-and-a-half year contract after United agreed to pay more than £10million ($13m) to buy him and his backroom staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation.

Before boarding his flight, Pochettino not only waved to his adoring fans, but took a photo with staff and players on the pitch in Cincinnati.

Industry observers note that 'It's impossible not to cry, but that is because we care about the people and the people care about us,' he told reporters. 'When that happens, it's normal to show your emotions, no? Because we are human. We are no robots.'.

Mauricio Pochettino saying his final goodbyes to the USA fans as he's now gonna fly to Manchester immediately ❤️ pic.twitter.com/sCe8LCjpK5.

Pulisic, perhaps Pochettino's brightest pupil, scored on a bicycle kick in the 25th minute.

Pulisic celebrates his goal on Tuesday night in Cincinnati during the win over Haiti.

Pochettino was expected to board a flight from northern Kentucky to Manchester after the win.

Sources indicate that pochettino had been on something of a farewell tour in the US, where he embraced the local sports scene over his brief tenure. In between overseeing his final games with the USMNT, Pochettino was spotted at the Cincinnati Bengals' win over the visiting Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday.

The manager, sporting his blue USSF coat, was captured standing on the sidelines with members of his staff ahead before kickoff, where he mingled with Bengals special teamers such as kicker Evan McPherson, long snapper William Wagner and punter Ryan Rehkow.

A night earlier, Pochettino guided the US to a 6-0 win over Haiti in Miami to give his team a safe cushion for his farewell on Tuesday in Cincinnati.

Pochettino broke down in tears as he revealed his decision last week, while admitting he couldn't turn down the 'dream' job with Manchester United.

Mauricio Pochettino walks on the field after the CONCACAF Nations League Quarterfinal.

American fans give Pochettino a standing ovation in Cincinnati after his farewell match.

Flanked by US Soccer Federation bosses at the team's headquarters in Georgia, an emotional Pochettino wiped away tears as he thanked the players and staff.

'I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,' he remarked. 'It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

'I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

Recent findings suggest that 'Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

Recent findings suggest that 'In some part it's a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'.

United will pay the US Soccer Federation more than $13.2 million (£10m) in compensation for Pochettino and his backroom staff.

Sources indicate that 'I never stated I wanted to go back in the Premier League,' Pochettino, a former Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton boss, told reporters last week. 'All of this was so quick because we arrived here last Friday and on Sunday afternoon this type of situation started to appear.'.

Pochettino turns his attention to an 18th-place United squad that has just one EPL win.

Mauricio Pochettino insisted it was the 'most difficult decision' to leave the USMNT.

Recent findings suggest that pochettino put together a 23-12-2 record with the US, while 78 players earned caps for the US over his tenure. Remarkably, nine teenagers made their USMNT debuts for Pochettino, including Hall, who scored on Tuesday.

But the Americans failed to crack into the sport's upper echelon during Pochettino's brief tenure in the US. In his lone World Cup appearance with the team last summer, Pochettino guided the USMNT to the Round of 16, where the Americans fell to Belgium, 4-1.

That result was an improvement on 2018, when the US failed to qualify, but not on 2022, when then-coach Gregg Berhalter's similarly team fell short of the quarters with a 3-1 loss to the Netherlands.

Despite this, Pochettino's American players have remained largely supportive of his tenure, including Berhalter's son Sebastian, who said the outgoing coach helped him 'develop as a player and as a person.'.

Prior to Tuesday's win, Pochettino thanked American fans for the support he received over his two years with the national team.

'Thank you so much from the bottom of my heart for all the fans, for all the people that was supporting us in the last two years,' Pochettino mentioned in a video posted on social media. 'Special, great memories of the World Cup and everything that we lived together. Always in my heart, always one of you. All the best and I wish everything good for the future.'.

Potential candidates to replace Pochettino in the US include former Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola, ex-England manager Gareth Southgate and some lesser-known candidates like Cherundolo, who now guides the United States U-23 team.

'For us to win, we need to be great at a lot of things, and we need someone who cares about youth development, cares about our youth national team programs, our relationships with our clubs and the success of the federation more broadly,' US Soccer CEO JT Batson told TNT Sports on Tuesday. 'We know that is a key part of our success, and it's also a key part of how we've been able to attract great people because they get to do significant things.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

Sources indicate that "I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," remarked Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

Recent findings suggest that "It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old mentioned.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams.".

It has been revealed that antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

Sources indicate that the final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

Former Manchester United and Chelsea star Juan Mata has retired from football at the age of 38.

After leaving Chelsea, the Spaniard enjoyed a strong stint at Manchester United.

At the end of last month, the Euro 2012 winner was treated to a lap of appreciation at his last club Melbourne Victory.

But a falling-out with then-coach Jose Mourinho called time on his stint at Stamford Bridge and a move north to join Man United – where he would later reunite with the Portuguese manager during his stint in Manchester between 2016 and 2018.

Mata later enjoyed stints at Galatasaray, Vissel Kobe and Western Sydney Wanderers before his move to Melbourne.

In recent years, however, Mata has expanded his career away from the pitch, with the player serving as a pundit at this year's World Cup for ITV, and at the 2024 European Championship for BBC Sport.

As well as appearing in the media, Mata is a keen investor in sporting ventures including Spanish club Real Oviedo, San Diego FC in the MLS and Formula One's Alpine racing team.

Alongside Italy icon Giorgio Chiellini, Mata is an investor in Mercury/13, a women's multi-club ownership group that invests in FC Como Women.

Mata is also a co-owner of Melbourne Victory, with plans to chair a football committee at the club after hanging up his boots.

As well as a shrewd businessman, Mata is also a philanthropist – and was recognised for his donations with an MBE in June 2025.

In 2017, Mata pledged one per cent of his salary to a charitable movement called Common Goal, which supports football charities.

#1591. Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 50 min read (9994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section.
  • Sources indicate that the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7.
  • For example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections1,2,3, and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips4. In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model5. The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

Sources indicate that the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7. In superfluids and superconductors, this breaking manifests in the emergence of a macroscopic condensate that exhibits long-range phase coherence. This coherence is ultimately responsible for properties such as dissipationless transport8,9, the Josephson effect10, and in the case of superconductivity the Meissner effect11. Although relatively robust in bulk systems, in lower-dimensional systems, the enhanced effect of fluctuations—and in particular topological defects—can suppress this long-range phase coherence and govern superfluid transport4,12.

For example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts. The supercurrent, proportional to this gradient, would grow without bound unless intermittent phase fluctuations relax the accumulated gradient. By relaxing the gradient, the fluctuations dissipate energy, thereby causing a resistance3,13. The characteristics of the fluctuations and their corresponding resistance depend on the dimensionality of the setup as follows.

In one-dimensional (1D) wires, discrete relaxation events known as phase slips dominate the dynamics. Microscopically, a phase slip occurs when the magnitude of the superconducting order parameter is transiently and locally suppressed over a healing length ξ. Where the amplitude vanishes, the phase is ill-defined, allowing for phase jumps of 2π. As the order parameter recovers, the wire returns to a state with a uniform amplitude but a reduced phase gradient4 (Fig. 1a, top row).

Recent findings suggest that a, Dissipation in a narrow, quasi-1D channel occurs because of phase slips, in which a depletion of the order parameter allows for a relaxation of the phase gradient and kinetic energy (top row). The corresponding phase (colour-coded) evolution of a phase slip in a narrow channel is plotted in the central row. In a wide, quasi-2D channel, dissipation is governed by vortex–antivortex pairs traversing the channel (bottom row). b, A transport channel of programmable width connects two superfluid reservoirs (blue). The channel is formed by two repulsive beams (green and orange), one of which is tunable by a DMD.

Sources indicate that in two-dimensional (2D) geometries, such as thin films, dissipation instead arises from the nucleation and motion of topological defects known as vortices. A vortex is a point-like singularity of the phase around which the phase winds by 2π, with a small core in which the amplitude is suppressed. Driven by a current, vortices move across the film and dissipate energy. Each time a vortex traverses the sample, the phase difference between the contacts relaxes by 2π. Repeated vortex crossings generate a finite voltage and hence an effective resistance14,15 (Fig. 1a, bottom row). In intermediate, thin-strip geometries, both vortex flow and phase slips may contribute to dissipation.

In a recent development, previous studies included experiments on superconducting rings16; Dayem-bridge nanowires17,18,19,20; Bose–Einstein condensates in dumbbell21,22, cylindrical23 or toroidal geometries24; optical lattices25,26; and fermionic Josephson junctions27,28,29. These previous studies have explored various facets of phase-slip and vortex physics, including direct imaging of vortices28,30,31,32, the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless phase transition33 and the recent observation of Shapiro steps in atomic Josephson junctions34,35. However, the experimental challenge of isolating and characterizing geometric or dimensional effects on dissipation remains unresolved.

With the rise of quantum simulation of devices based on highly controllable ultracold atomic gases36,37, it is now possible to shed new light on how these dissipative processes emerge in quantum systems.

Recent findings suggest that in this work, we use ultracold, strongly interacting fermions in a two-terminal configuration to study nonlinear transport through a digitally programmable channel. The optically shaped channel can be reproducibly tuned from a quasi-1D to a quasi-2D geometry, providing a platform ideally suited for probing the influence of geometry on fluctuation-driven dissipation in the absence of defects or impurities.

Sources indicate that in the narrow, 1D channel limit, we identify signatures of phase slips, in agreement with the Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin (LAMH) theory4,38,39. In particular, we observe the predicted exponential suppression of the LAMH activation factor over many orders of magnitude on widening the channel. For even larger widths, the system crosses over to a 2D regime in which dissipation is dominated by vortices, as indicated by the observed power-law dependence of the current–voltage characteristics predicted for vortex dynamics.

Recent findings suggest that beyond establishing these limiting behaviours, our measurements provide a direct window into the crossover between 1D and 2D transport, a regime in which analytical modelling is challenging. It is in this crossover that widening the channel paradoxically increases its resistance. More broadly, our results highlight the utility of ultracold atomic superfluids as a platform for quantum simulation of nonequilibrium transport.

In a recent development, we prepare a balanced mixture of the lowest and third-lowest hyperfine states of fermionic 6Li in the unitary regime. A total of 2N = 2.7 ± 0.1 × 105 atoms are cooled to T/TF = 0.144 ± 0.007, where N denotes the number of atom pairs, TF denotes the Fermi temperature, and the errors in both quantities denote the uncertainties due to shot-to-shot fluctuations. The temperature corresponds to T/TC ≈ 0.7, where TC ≈ 0.2TF denotes the critical temperature40. The atoms are confined in a cigar-shaped, harmonic trap with trapping frequencies (νx, νy, νz) = (222 ± 7, 28.1 ± 0.1, 195 ± 5) Hz.

It has been revealed that as shown in Fig. 1a, a repulsive TEM0,1 beam, propagating in the x-direction, is aligned with the trap centre. It divides the atomic cloud into two reservoirs, separated by a quasi-2D transport region that is 51 ± 1 μm long and provides confinement of ν2D = 10.46 ± 0.09 kHz along z. Within the central 27 ± 0.5 μm of this plane, the atoms are further confined in the x-direction to a channel of variable width w. The channel is defined by a repulsive beam propagating along z, shaped by a digital micromirror device (DMD). It enables reproducible tunability of w from 0.9 ± 0.5 μm to 19.8 ± 0.5 μm, in which the uncertainty is dominated by and calculated from the resolution limit of our projection system (numerical aperture = 0.53, λ = 532 nm). Note that given the dimensions of our setup, we are not in the Josephson regime (see Methods, ‘No Josephson oscillations’). A third, attractive Gaussian beam (not shown) illuminates the transport channel and its connections to the reservoirs, locally increasing the degeneracy. A more detailed description of this effect as well as of the overall setup can be found in ref. 41.

In a recent development, at time t = 0, we prepare a relative atom-pair imbalance between the two reservoirs, ΔN/N = (Nl − Nr)/(Nl + Nr), where Nl,r denote the number of atom pairs in the left and right reservoirs. An initial imbalance of ΔN/N ≈ 0.1 relaxes through an approximately constant initial current, followed by damped oscillations of the imbalance. The discharge is distinctly non-exponential, indicating a nonlinear response. The damping, and in particular its dependence on the channel width w, carries information about the underlying microscopic mechanisms.

The key data of our measurement series are shown in Fig. 2a. We record transport traces for w between 0.9 ± 0.5 μm and 19.8 ± 0.5 μm. As w increases, the magnitude of the initial current increases, which manifests in a steeper initial slope. Concurrently, both the oscillation frequency and amplitude grow. The frequency rises from just below 10 Hz to approximately 18 Hz (see also Extended Data Fig. 1). For the narrowest channel (w = 0.9 ± 0.5 μm), the oscillation amplitude is comparable to the noise floor and barely resolved. By contrast, for the widest channel (w = 19.8 ± 0.5 μm), the amplitude reaches ΔN/N ≈ 0.06.

a, Atom transport (imbalance ΔN/N as a function of time t) of a unitary Fermi gas through channels of increasing width indicates distinctively changing dissipation characteristics. The data are compared with fitted phase slip (LAMH) and vortex models. The models both describe the TNR in the circuit (b), capturing either phase slips or vortices. The LAMH model fits narrow channels, whereas the vortex model fits wide channels. The measurements for different channel widths are vertically offset for clarity. The statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically four to five measurements per data point) are smaller than the marker size. c, A quality-of-fit \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis substantiates the change of the dominant model apparent in a.

According to recent reports, the damping exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on w. At longer transport times (for example, t = 0.3 s), the remaining oscillation amplitude reaches a maximum for intermediate channel widths (see also Fig. 4). These signals suggest distinct dissipative mechanisms in the narrow and wide channel limits, which we analyse quantitatively below.

According to recent reports, the general characteristics of the dynamics can be understood as arising from the interplay between the potential energy stored in the reservoirs, the kinetic energy inside the channel and the dissipative processes we want to investigate. To study these dissipative processes, we model our system with an equivalent RLC circuit shown in Fig. 2b. We first characterize the capacitance and inductance of the circuit to subsequently infer the dissipative (resistive) processes by fitting the dynamics of the circuit to the measurements. The capacitances, inductance and resistance in the circuit model correspond to the compressibility of the atomic reservoirs, the inertia of the atoms and the dissipative processes in the channel, respectively. We explore these elements in the following starting with the capacitors. As the model circuit features two capacitors in series, each with a capacitance C, the effective capacitance of the circuit is Ceff = C/2. The compressibility κeff of the gas allows to quantify this equivalent capacitance Ceff (potential energy per atom pair displaced from equilibrium) through \(\frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{\kappa }_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta {E}_{\mathrm{pot}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{C}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). We measured the compressibility of our sample (Methods, ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) to find hCeff = 15.8 ± 0.5 s, where h is Planck’s constant. Next we quantify the inductance. To do so, we assume all channels have box-like potentials. A charge-neutral atom-pair current I carries a kinetic energy Ekin that depends on w. We define the inductance of our systems using \({E}_{{\rm{kin}}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}L{I}^{2}.\) We developed a model that predicts a functional dependence.

Recent findings suggest that (Methods, ‘Derivation of the inductance’). By analysing the oscillation frequencies observed in our measurements and noting that in a weakly damped circuit, the frequencies are given by \(\omega (w)\approx 1/\sqrt{L(w){C}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\), we find ℓc/h = 3.01 ± 0.03 × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06 ± 0.04 × 10−6 s. Although the details are provided in the Supplementary Information, here we state that the first term in equation (1) captures the kinetic energy in the channel, whereas the second term accounts for the kinetic energy in the reservoirs.

According to recent reports, phase slips and vortices dissipate the kinetic energy of the current into heat. So, they effectively act as a topological nonlinear resistor (TNR). With L and C determined, the resistance R remains the sole unknown component in our circuit. Owing to the nature of phase slips, R is topological and nonlinear, meaning it depends not only on the geometry but also on the current.

Showing how R depends on geometry, in particular in relation to the length scale given by ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’), reveals the nature of the underlying dissipative processes. To do so, we fit the width-dependent resistance R(w) in the equations of motion of an RLC circuit (derived in Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’).

For narrow, quasi-1D channels (w ≱ 2ξ), we expect the system to be in the phase slip regime. The LAMH model predicts4.

Recent findings suggest that defined using R = V/I, where R0 is the characteristic resistance, w0 is the characteristic width, and I0 = 2kBT/h, where kB is the Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature. The exponential suppression of R with w reflects the thermally activated phase-slip rate scaling with \(\varGamma \propto \exp (-\Delta F/({k}_{{\rm{B}}}T))\) (ref. 18), where the free energy barrier for phase slips is ΔF ∝ w. The sinh(I/I0) term can intuitively be understood as follows: at small |I/I0| ≪ 1, phase slips occur in both directions with roughly equal probability; as the bias increases slightly, phase slips that relax the current become more probable. For large |I/I0| ≫ 1, sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2. reflecting the local destabilization of the superfluid and the resulting exponential increase in the phase-slip probability.

Using our predetermined C and L(w), we determine R0 and w0 by fitting them simultaneously to the measurements of our four narrowest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’). Assuming that the LAMH model can be used to describe our system, a simultaneous fit to multiple channel widths provides a robust extraction of the model parameters but enforces the predicted exponential suppression of RLAMH with w. We find R0/h = 102.3±0.2 and w0 = 49.7(6) nm, where the errors denote the uncertainties of the fit. The resulting fits (shown in Fig. 2a) largely capture the dynamics for channels with a width up to w = 2.5 μm. This is quantified by \(\mathrm{NRMSE}\,=\) \(\sqrt{{\sum }_{i}{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}/N}/({m}_{\max }-{m}_{\min }) < 0.06\), where mi and fi denote the measured and fitted imbalances, respectively, and mmax − mmin is the measured signal range. However, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis \(({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 9)\) shown in Fig. 2c suggests additional systematic effects beyond the very small statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically on the level of 0.004). These systematic effects could originate from the approximation of modelling the channel with a box-like potential or the attractive beam illuminating the channel locally increasing the temperature. Outside the validity range of the model, the quality of the fits degrades noticeably, failing to capture the phase of the oscillations and underestimating their damping.

It has been revealed that in a second step, we validate the choice of the LAMH model by fitting RLAMH(w) to each curve individually. In contrast to the simultaneous fit, these individual fits do not enforce the predicted scaling RLAMH(w) and therefore provide an independent test of whether the scaling is present in the data. Within the validity regime of the model, the individual fits reproduce the predicted exponential scaling over many orders of magnitude, as shown in Fig. 3a.

a, The fitted phase-slip resistance RLAMH(w), for narrow channels, demonstrates the exponential suppression with width, as predicted by LAMH theory. b, The fitted vortex resistivity ρv(w), for wide channels, shows the predicted power law. Inside the crossover region (2–4ξ), that is, outside the validity range of the models, both scalings break down (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’). Note that a and b display different quantities (resistance compared with resistivity) characterizing different regimes (1D compared with 2D) and are therefore not intended to be compared across the dimensional crossover. The error bars represent the error of the fit.

Industry observers note that this is the first main finding of this paper. Compared with RLAMH(w), the total resistance R(I, w) apparent in the measurements (Fig. 2a) varies much less. As we initialize a fixed potential bias in our system, the exponential geometric suppression (R ∝ exp(−w/w0)) approximately cancels the current-induced exponential enhancement (R ∝ sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2). This allows RLAMH to be inferred over a wide range—more than 10 decades—while only exploring a relatively modest dynamic range of R. Importantly, the observed scaling of RLAMH(w) is contained within the data itself and is not just an artefact of the choice of the model. This becomes evident when the model is applied outside its validity regime, where the scaling breaks down immediately (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’).

In quasi-2D channels (w ≳ 4ξ), phase slips become energetically unfavourable, as their activation energy increases exponentially with w. Instead, dissipation is expected to be governed by vortex flow. Owing to the vortices, we expect to see a power-law dependence in the pair-current density J:.

Recent findings suggest that where J0 = I0/ξ. A derivation, building on the results of ref. 5, is provided in the Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’. By fitting α and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) simultaneously to the data of our four widest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’), we find \(\alpha =1.98\pm 0.04,{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \sim }}_{0}/h=1{0}^{-4.79\pm 0.07}\). As apparent from Fig. 2a, this model captures the dynamics for channels in the 2D regime (NRMSE ≱ 0.06). In these cases, \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 4\). Note that the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, and for wide channels, the box-potential approximation is safer compared with narrow channels. Apart from these statistical tests, we validate our model by fixing α to its global fit value but fitting ρv to each individual curve. Within the validity range of the model, these individual fits agree with the predicted power-law ρv ∝ wα−1 (Fig. 3b). This scaling is the second main finding of the paper. The scaling breaks down outside the validity regime of the model (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’), providing evidence that the observed scaling is a feature of the data, not a mere artefact of the enforced power law R ∝ Jα−1. When approaching the dimensional crossover w ≱ 4ξ, while still largely capturing the dynamics, the model begins to slightly but systematically underestimate the amplitude of the oscillations at long times. Presumably, because the approximation of sufficiently large w used in the derivation of R(J) ceases to hold (Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’). The eventual breakdown of the vortex model at w ≈ 4ξ marks the end of the 2D regime: the vortex model should be valid only when vortex–antivortex pairs are available as excitations. As each vortex has a radius of ξ, such an excitation requires w ≳ 4ξ. This leaves a gap between the validity ranges of the phase slip and the vortex model, in which neither model provides a microscopically satisfactory description. In this gap, there is a dimensional crossover, in which both phase slips and vortices compete.

The underdamped oscillations allow us to characterize dissipation in our system using only a few basic assumptions, while staying agnostic to the dissipation mechanism. This is particularly useful to analyse the dimensional crossover, in which neither the phase-slip nor the vortex model provide a satisfactory microscopical description. We split the total energy Etot into a potential (capacitive) energy EC and a kinetic (inductive) energy EL. We assume Etot = EC(ΔN) + EL(I, w) with EC ∝ ΔN2 and EL(I = 0, w) = 0. For each channel width w, we extract the times ti,w at which ΔN(t = ti, w) reaches an extremum and thus I ≈ 0. There, the system has minimal inductive energy (EL ≈ 0) and maximal capacitive energy. The fraction of the initial energy remaining in the system is then given by.

The remaining energy as a function of time and channel width is shown in Fig. 4. The plot is obtained by cubic interpolation between the measured points, performed linearly in time and logarithmically in width.

The remaining energy in the oscillator paradoxically varies non-monotonically as a function of the channel width w. For a given time after the initial decay, the maximum appears in the crossover region, near w = 4 μm ≈ 3ξ, in which phase slips and vortices are suppressed but competing. The crosses mark the measurement points (typically four to five measurements per cross) between which we interpolate. We estimate the individual data points to have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a statistical uncertainty smaller than 2% (Methods, ‘Error estimation’).

According to recent reports, for a fixed width, the energy decays over time, reflecting dissipation. At any given time t > 0.15 s, Et(w)/E0 varies non-monotonically with the channel width, exhibiting a clear maximum near w ≈ 3ξ, corresponding to a minimal effective resistance. We call this deviation from the expected monotonicity the ‘quantum resistance paradox’ and consider it the third and last main finding of this paper. Note that the activation energy for phase slips increases exponentially with channel width, whereas vortex–antivortex pairs require sufficiently wide channels to form. The observed non-monotonicity thus suggests a transition in the underlying dissipation mechanism and a crossover from 1D to 2D physics.

We have investigated atom transport between two bulk superfluids through channels across different dimensional regimes and observed distinct behaviours. In narrow, quasi-1D channels, our data are in agreement with those of the LAMH model. We infer the geometric suppression of the phase slips by many orders of magnitude, providing the first experimental confirmation of the predicted geometric scaling. For wide, quasi-2D channels, dissipation is captured by a vortex flow model. The borders of the 1D and 2D regimes appear close to the theoretically expected length scale. A measurement of energy decay, agnostic to microscopic details, provides further evidence for a transition in the dissipation mechanism for channels of intermediate width, which paradoxically exhibit the least energy loss. These findings not only suggest routes for optimizing energy transport in mesoscopic devices but also provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts to describe the delicate phase-slip and vortex-flow mechanisms in the dimensional crossover in superfluids and superconductors42,43,44.

Our setup is analogous to an RLC circuit with the mapping presented in Extended Data Table 1.

It has been revealed that the procedures for determining the capacitance C and the inductance L are described in sections ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’ and ‘Derivation of the inductance’. Here, we derive the governing equations and provide additional details on the fitting procedure used to determine R, as presented in the main text.

The total number of atoms in each reservoir is measured directly using absorption images of both hyperfine states (|1⟩ and |3⟩), taken in rapid succession. To determine the total number of pairs in each reservoir Nl,r, we use both measurements, as this reduces statistical uncertainty. Specifically, \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}}}=({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|1\rangle }+{N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|3\rangle })/2\), where \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|i\rangle }\) denotes the number of atoms in the left and right reservoirs in state |i⟩. However, the second image (state |3⟩) demonstrates a cloud that has absorbed some energy from the first imaging pulse and is therefore slightly distorted. To avoid systematic effects from this distortion on C and T, we use only the image of the lowest hyperfine state (|1⟩) to extract the compressibility and temperature of the cloud, assuming these are identical for both states. We verified that our preparation is equivalent for both states by inverting the imaging sequence. We describe our system in terms of pairs and report C, L and R for pairs and pair currents, respectively.

In a recent development, as shown in Fig. 2b, our RLC circuit consists of two capacitors (reservoirs) in series. We replace these two capacitors C by an effective capacitance Ceff = C/2. With this replacement, we obtain a standard RLC series circuit with an initially charged capacitor but no externally applied voltage.

Experimentally, transport is initiated by ramping down a blue-detuned beam that blocks the channel. A sudden quench of this beam slightly perturbs the reservoirs, so we instead ramp it down over 10 ms. This introduces an unknown initial condition I(t = 0). For each curve, we fit I(t = 0) ∈ [0, Iavg], where Iavg is the average current during the initial decay (before oscillations). To avoid giving undue weight to the first measured point, we fit ΔNfit(t = 0) ∈ [0.8, 1.2] ⋅ ΔNmeasured(t = 0). These bounds are necessary to prevent the models from ignoring the initial decay outside their validity regime. In particular, this is the case for the LAMH model when fitting data of wide channels, where only a few points represent the initial dynamics.

For numerical stability, R0 and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) are fitted on a logarithmic scale, whereas α and w0 are fitted linearly.

It has been revealed that finally, we discuss the fitting weights. Each configuration (t, w) has five measurements. Points with preparation errors (low atom number) are excluded, typically leaving four to five measurements per point and occasionally three. The experimental standard deviation is calculated for each configuration individually. We assume that for a given w, the uncertainty is independent of t. To prevent the fit from being dominated by points with unrealistically small uncertainties, both the fitting and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) calculations replace individual error bars with the median error bar of all the data sharing w.

It has been revealed that the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis shown in Fig. 2c is performed as follows. The uncertainty of the measured points is assumed to be identical for all points belonging to a specific channel width. For each channel width, the model is fitted, either with 2.5 effective degrees of freedom (R0, w0, ΔN0, I0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0},\alpha ,\Delta {N}_{0},{I}_{0}\)), where the first two parameters are shared among four channels (2/4 = 0.5) if the channel participates in the global fit of the respective model, or two degrees of freedom (ΔN0, I0) otherwise. The reduced chi-squared is then calculated using \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}=\frac{1}{n-m}\sum \frac{{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}}{{\sigma }^{2}}\), where mi are the measured values, fi the corresponding values fitted by the model, σ the uncertainty shared by all measurement points of a specific width, n the number of measured points and m = 2.5 or m = 2 the number of effectively fitted degrees of freedom.

We discuss how the fitted models are affected by the various sources of systematic uncertainty. Specifically, we investigate how systematic uncertainties in the capacitance C, the channel width w and the temperature T affect the quality of the model fits and the inferred parameters RLAMH and α.

In a recent development, assume that the true physical capacitance \(\widetilde{C}\) differs from the calculated value (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) by a factor γ, such that \(C=\gamma \widetilde{C}\). In our analysis, the effective inductance L is determined (see section ‘Derivation of the inductance’) before fitting the resistance by analysing the underdamped, multi-period oscillations of the system. Owing to the observation of multiple periods, the frequency can be measured with good accuracy and precision. A systematic shift γ ≠ 1 would therefore result in an inverse scaling of the extracted inductance curve, \(L\approx \widetilde{L}/\gamma \), where \(\widetilde{L}\) represents the true physical inductance. Inspecting the underlying equation of motion of the circuit (equation (2)) demonstrates that the extracted resistance scales identically with this factor (R ∝ 1/γ). This uniform rescaling by 1/α can be absorbed in the prefactor R0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\), leaving the quality of the fits, scalings, the inferred dynamic ranges and the geometric suppression constant w0 entirely unaffected.

According to recent reports, the geometric potential landscape is projected onto the atoms using a DMD. Although physical pixel spacing and optical demagnification ratio are known accurately, the primary source of spatial uncertainty stems from the finite resolution of the imaging optics. The finite resolution effectively blurs the repulsive potential walls of the channel. Consequently, having to choose where to define the sharp boundaries of the model (spaced by w) within this blurred profile introduces a systematic uncertainty Δw.

It has been revealed that importantly, this geometric uncertainty of roughly 0.5 μm is expected to be shared across all channel configurations and does not affect each channel independently of the others. For channels in the 1D regime, the initial discharge through the narrowest channels is characterized by an extended period of nearly constant current in which inertial forces are negligible (∣L dI/dt∣ ≪ |RI|). In this regime, the system behaves predominantly as a nonlinear RC circuit, approximately decoupling the resistance fit from the precise value of L. Then, a uniform translation of w by Δw alters the resistances by a constant factor. For the LAMH model, \(R(w+\Delta w)\propto \exp (-\Delta w/{w}_{0})\). Similarly to the capacitance error, this effect is entirely absorbed by a re-normalization of the global prefactor R0, preserving both the dynamic range of RLAMH and its slope set by w0. The relatively high value of \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) for the LAMH model might be caused by the experiment that violates the assumption of box-like channel potentials. For the channels in the 2D regime, Δw/w ≪ 1, so we expect systematic effects caused by Δw ≠ 0 to be small and the approximation of modelling the channels as box-like to be safe.

It has been revealed that although we calibrated our measurements with the thermodynamic reference point of Bose–Einstein condensation, our measured atom-pair numbers and temperatures (see sections ‘High-saturation imaging’ and ‘Thermodynamic state extraction by 2D equation of state fitting’) might be subject to systematic errors. An error in the inferred pair-number \(N=\gamma \widetilde{N}\), where N is the inferred particle number and \(\widetilde{N}\) is the physical particle number, would force a corresponding shift in C, thereby rescaling L and R as discussed above. Moreover, it would rescale I. As the current enters the expression for the resistance in the vortex model only in the form of a power law, it would merely shift \(\widetilde{R}\) by a constant factor γ−α. Again, this constant factor would affect neither α, nor the quality of the vortex-model fits, nor the quality of its scaling law. As the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, it is unaffected by potential systematic effects in T. For the LAMH model, the situation is different. The temperature enters the model explicitly through I0 = 2kBT/h. Variations in both N and T ultimately tie into the ratio I/I0. Because this ratio controls the degree of nonlinearity of the circuit, we can model their combined systematic impact by analysing variations in I0 alone.

Sources indicate that the initial discharge of the narrowest channels is distinctly nonlinear (implying I ≫ I0), whereas the subsequent oscillations are approximately sinusoidal (implying I ≱ I0). Consequently, the ratio I/I0 is constrained by the geometric profile of the relaxation curves. However, systematic effects that affect the ratio I/I0 do also affect the quality of fit and the dynamic range of RLAMH. In general, if I/I0 is lowered (by decreasing I or increasing T), the circuit is less nonlinear and the dynamic range of RLAMH decreases, whereas an increase in the ratio has the opposite effect. Although the parameter I0 is constrained in the LAMH model, we performed additional fittings, where I0 was a global fit parameter, to effectively account for potential systematic errors in I or T. The best fits are achieved with I0,fit = 3.50(1)I0, reducing \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) averaged over the five narrowest channels, by more than a factor of 2. A possible cause for this could be that the attractive Gaussian beam illuminating the channel locally heats the channel, thereby increasing I0. Note that this beam also increases the local degeneracy such that we would still expect the channel to be deeply degenerate. Although in the case of fitted I0, the dynamic range of RLAMH is reduced, it continues to span more than four orders of magnitude. The values are still in good agreement with the predicted exponential scaling.

As mentioned in section ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’, we measure only the atom number in one hyperfine state, so we use \(C\leftrightarrow \partial {N}_{|1\rangle }/\partial \mu ={\kappa }_{|1\rangle }\).

It is crucial to distinguish between the absolute atom number N and the differential capacitance κ. For the absolute atom number (equation (23)), we rely on numerical integration of the image because the presence of the wall beam approximately halves the relevant volume of the cloud. However, for the capacitance (κ = ∂N/∂μ), performing a numerical derivative on the noisy integrated signal would yield an unstable result. Sources indicate that for all channel widths except the narrowest one, we observe underdamped, long-lived oscillations. As these oscillations remain underdamped, the influence of the nonlinear resistance on the oscillation frequency is expected to be small. To extract the inductance of the channel for each width (except the narrowest one), we exclude the initial transient dynamics up to the first, global minimum occurring at a time t = t1,w. The remaining data are fitted with a damped sinusoidal function \({f}_{w}(t)={A}_{w}\exp (-(t-{t}_{1,w})/{\tau }_{w})\sin ({\omega }_{w}t+{\phi }_{{\rm{w}}})+\Delta {N}_{w,\mathrm{offset}},\) where Aw, τw, ωw, ϕw, and ΔNw,offset are fitting parameters. Small offsets |ΔNw,offset| < 0.018 account for potential alignment errors that cause the oscillations to centre around slightly nonzero values. Using the inferred effective capacitance Ceff of our circuit (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’), we determine the total inductance for a given channel width as \({L}_{w}=1/(({\omega }_{w}^{2}+{\tau }_{w}^{-2}){C}_{\mathrm{eff}})\approx 1/({\omega }_{w}^{2}C),\) where the approximation is equivalent to the result for an undamped LC circuit and holds for weakly damped circuits. Although the quantitative difference in our case is minute, we do include the τ-term capturing the effect of the resistance lowering the oscillation frequency of the RLC circuit. Note that for the wide channels in particular, fitting a damped sine to the oscillatory data is a pragmatic choice that allows for an approximation of the inductance, the signature of which is primarily contained in the frequency of the oscillation. Over extended periods of time, however, the damped sine and the dynamics of the vortex model would appear different, as the latter does not feature an exponentially decaying amplitude. This kinetic inductance Lw quantifies the kinetic energy associated with a given pair current I. Although the main contribution arises from the transport channel itself, there is also a residual contribution because of particle motion in the adjoining 2D and 3D regions, whose geometries are independent of the channel width. We therefore write \(L(w)={L}_{\mathrm{channel}}(w)+{L}_{\mathrm{res}}\). Assuming a constant particle density inside the channel, the mass of particles in the transport channel (M) scales with its width, M ∝ w. For a given current, the corresponding particle velocity in the channel thus scales inversely, \({v}_{\mathrm{channel}}\propto \frac{1}{w}\). Consequently, the kinetic energy associated with a fixed I scales as \({E}_{\mathrm{kin}}=M{v}_{\mathrm{channel}}^{2}/2\propto w{(1/w)}^{2}=1/w\), implying that Lchannel(w) ∝ 1/w. We therefore model the total inductance as.

with fitting parameters ℓc and Lres. We find ℓc/h = 3.01(3) × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06(4) × 10−6 s, where the uncertainties represent the standard errors of the fit. The measured inductances Lw and the fitted model are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. The excellent agreement of the model with the data validates our model assumptions.

In a previous, comparable experimental setting, we estimated the atoms traversing a region of length d ≈ 3 μm in a time t ≈ 330 μs, resulting in an estimated atomic velocity of v ≈ 9 mm s−1 (ref. 48). As our channel is practically defect free, we assume that the atomic velocity is close to the critical velocity vc. So we estimate 4ξ ≈ 4ħ/(mvc) ≈ 5 μm (ref. 49).

Sources indicate that given the method with which we extract the energy ratio, two main sources of error are to be considered. The first one is the statistical noise of the measurement points. This directly translates into an uncertainty of the inferred energy ratio but also causes a systematic bias towards higher values, as only the extrema of the signals are considered. The second contribution comes from the finite sampling rate of the oscillations. This causes an uncertainty and a bias towards lower values, as the measured points do not sample the peaks exactly. To quantitatively assess their influence for all our measurements, we performed Monte Carlo simulations. Specifically, we sampled sinusoidal signals with the frequencies, amplitudes and dampings observed in the signals used for Fig. 4. We sampled these artificial signals with the sampling rates and statistical noise that occurred in the physical experiment. This simulation yielded the following insight: For the data presented in Fig. 4, the inferred energies have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a standard deviation smaller than 2%.

Sources indicate that although several studies have reported on Josephson oscillations with seemingly similar measurements in comparable settings27,28,29, our system operates far outside the Josephson regime. The Josephson effect requires the junction length to be much shorter than the superconducting coherence length, which for our system is close to the healing length4,12. In our case, the channel length ℓ = 27 μm is much larger than the estimated healing length ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’). Moreover, we observe neither a well-defined current-phase relation nor an oscillation amplitude consistent with the Josephson relation. The former statement is based on time-of-flight measurements of the relative phase of the two reservoirs with the same preparation performed in a slightly different geometry. Although for the data shown in this manuscript, we always observe the same initial dynamics (up to small noise), these additional measurements confirm that the prepared phase between the two reservoirs is not controlled, sampling values between 0 and 2π from a flat distribution. We therefore conclude that the oscillatory signal observed in our experiment cannot be attributed to JO.

Industry observers note that extended Data Fig. 2 provides additional data related to Fig. 3. The theoretical motivation and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis presented in Fig. 2 already justify the choice of models. The data shown here complements that analysis by demonstrating that the scaling laws reported in Fig. 3 are not numerical artefacts and are not imposed by the fitting procedure.

For both the LAMH and vortex models, the predicted scalings break down outside their respective ranges of validity. This behaviour indicates that the observed scaling is not a numerical consequence of the fitting procedure and is not artificially enforced by the functional form of the models.

The saturation of the LAMH-inferred resistance at large widths does not seem to be due to limited fitting precision, fitting boundaries or lack of convergence. Instead, it reflects a transition from the strong exponential width dependence characteristic of the LAMH model to a much weaker dependence, as predicted by the vortex model.

For the vortex model, the trend reverses in the crossover regime, showing a clear deviation from the scaling expected by that model.

LA communities kick out Significant Oil

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .
  • "Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," remarked local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.
  • The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," remarked local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

According to recent reports, "In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.".

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property.".

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

It has been revealed that california's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Industry observers note that today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," mentioned Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman mentioned energy companies were prepared to challenge the fresh ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," remarked Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

Industry observers note that but those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is claims both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Henry Pollock was at the centre of an East Midlands derby flare-up that sparked a second-half Leicester onslaught as Northampton were overpowered at a sodden Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

The England back row, never knowingly far from controversy, escalated a brawl at the end of the first half that Leicester prop Joe Heyes revealed “added fuel to the fire” of a Tigers side who roared impressively when they returned after the break.

The incident fired up a sell-out crowd and Leicester brought what had up to that point been a drab game to life with a storming second-half performance.

Three tries in a pulverising 13-minute spell overturned a half-time deficit and put the hosts on course for a bonus-point win over their arch-rivals that took them to second place in the Prem table.

Pollock, withdrawn after 52 minutes, may wish to reflect on the wisdom of riling the Tigers in their own lair.

“That was a proper Tigers second half and a really pleasing performance,” Geoff Parling, their director of rugby, remarked.

Sources indicate that “We got on the front foot and showed our power. The way the guys problem-solved was brilliant and I’m just really pleased with the emotional energy they threw into that game.

“The way we were physically for each other – I’m really pleased.

“The challenge for us, if we want to be a title-winning team, is to play like that when it isn’t Northampton Saints. We have to play with that heart – the fire we showed in our chests – but also the calmness we showed too.

“I think if we play our game to the best of our ability we can knock over anyone.”.

It’s a big day for Alex Coles, who celebrates his milestone 150th cap today.

The 27-year-old lock follows Fraser Dingwall, Rory Hutchinson and Alex Mitchell to become the fourth member of Saints’ current squad to reach 150 appearances for his boyhood club, eight years after making his debut in 2018.

Coles marks one of nine changes to Saints’ side for the Derby Day clash, with Emmanuel Iyogun, Curtis Langdon, Ed Prowse, Tom Pearson and Henry Pollock the other names coming into the forward pack.

Cleopas Kundiona retains his place in the front row while milestone man Coles joins Prowse in the second row against Tigers.

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the newly introduced campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

According to recent reports, tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back promptly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” stated Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”.

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”.

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

In a recent development, kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

Sitting sixth in the top-flight table and heading into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals next month, Barry notes there’s a feel-good factor around the Club at the moment.

Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, declared shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again.
  • "Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," mentioned Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, declared shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," mentioned Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities," he stated. "We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions.".

It has been revealed that the first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment.".

Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament.

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he mentioned in a statement.

Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim in May.

"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.

"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly.".

The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

Recent findings suggest that "I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.

Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

Sources indicate that the International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.

The Kremlin's reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

Recent findings suggest that "Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations is now emerging as a real possibility.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday evening.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

By Tuesday afternoon, the Finland-led effort was gaining steam, with Sweden, Norway and Denmark making similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said in a statement.

This came shortly after Norway remarked it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

Sources indicate that "Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors tournament.

There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.

Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all.".

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

It has been revealed that this article was originally published on November 2, 2026. It was updated on November 3 with the statement from the Finnish Ice Hockey Association. It was later updated with the statements from the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish federations.

They want an opportunity to ensure that he has a say in what could be a life-changing decision.

Gabriel has been training in Madrid and gave an interview to Marca earlier this month saying that he favoured a move to the 15-time European champions over rivals Barcelona, while expressing an ambition to win the Ballon d’Or.

Manchester United are prepared for a legal fight with Real Madrid over JJ Gabriel.

The youngster is on the verge of joining the Spanish giants in a controversial move.

Sources indicate that he is registered as a United player for the rest of the season and the club are refusing to tear up that agreement in the belief that he would still need approval from FIFA to make the move. However, sources stress that there has been no contact from any football authority seeking to de-register him.

It has been revealed that gabriel has been at United since the age of 11, and is considered one of the hottest young prospects in European football. He is registered with United's academy until the end of the season but Real Madrid are intending to sign him in January.

There is a FIFA loophole that allows European clubs to tie down young players to professional contracts if they have a European passport which Gabriel qualifies for through both parents.

It has been revealed that in a farewell post on Instagram he remarked: 'Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020. as a 10-year-old boy with major dreams.

In a recent development, 'Here I grew as a player and as a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.

Gabriel did not make a competitive first-team appearance for United, but did make a senior appearance in United's pre-season friendly defeat to AC Milan this summer.

United’s hierarchy were left unsure what triggered his request to leave given he had become a key part of plans in first team training sessions this season.

United were left rocked in September when Gabriel's family unexpectedly requested to cancel his contract with immediate effect.

Daily Mail Sport revealed at the time that United’s hierarchy were left unsure what triggered such a move given he had become a key part of plans in first team training sessions this season under Michael Carrick.
